title: resourceClaimTemplate in Pod.Spec is changed to nil when the manifest is submitted to api-server
body:
### What happened?

I set the dra feature-gate to true in kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager, kubelet and kube-scheduler. and set the runtime-config to `api/all` for the api-server.

- kube-apiserver:

```
    - --feature-gates=DynamicResourceAllocation=true
    - --runtime-config=api/all=true
```

- kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler:

```
    - --feature-gates=DynamicResourceAllocation=true
```

I created the daemonset and configure the resourceClaims in pod.spec, see below:

```
      resourceClaims:
      - name: demo-static
        resourceClaimTemplateName: demo-static
```

and I submitted the daemonset.yaml:

title: ConfigMap SubPath Volume Mount failed on `util-linux=2.41`
body:
### What happened?

Mount command executes failed when creating a Pod using ConfigMap SubPath volume after upgrading `util-linux` to `2.41`.

`kubectl describe pod` Events: 

```log
Error: failed to generate container "ddcc1d587faca0a37bc7ee0bf46abbf7ce009c31a838f00f7a2a640667b713da" spec: failed to generate spec: failed to mkdir "/var/lib/kubelet/pods/ed5ba81a-2777-4ac9-a986-33238d803bdf/volume-subpaths/config/demo/0": mkdir /var/lib/kubelet/pods/ed5ba81a-2777-4ac9-a986-33238d803bdf/volume-subpaths/config/demo/0: file exists

> The `dmesg` does not show any error messages related to the `mount` command. 

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/34ea22cb-484b-4a1d-b958-1358ff59dc25

### What did you expect to happen?

Pod using ConfigMap SubPath volumes should be created successfully.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Bump `util-linux` version `2.41`.
    ````console
    # pacman -Si util-linux
    Repository      : core
    Name            : util-linux
    Version         : 2.41-2
    ....
    ````
2. Install K3s or RKE2.
    ```bash
    # export INSTALL_K3S_MIRROR=cn   # Uncomment if install K3s in China regions.
    curl -sfL https://rancher-mirror.rancher.cn/k3s/k3s-install.sh | \
        INSTALL_K3S_VERSION=v1.31.6+k3s1 \
        sh -s - server \
        --cluster-init

    # After the K3s server ready
    mkdir -p ~/.kube/config
    cat /etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml > ~/.kube/config
    ```
3. Apply the following example ConfigMap and Pod configuration.
```yaml
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: test
data:
  test.conf: |
    AAA=FOO
    BBB=BAR
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test
spec:
  containers:
    - name: demo
      image: alpine
      command: ["sleep", "3600"]
      volumeMounts:
      - name: config
        mountPath: "/config"
        subPath: "test.conf"
  volumes:
  # You set volumes at the Pod level, then mount them into containers inside that Pod
  - name: config
    configMap:
      # Provide the name of the ConfigMap you want to mount.
      name: test
      items:
        - key: test.conf
          path: test.conf

```
4. Pod failed to create with following error in events.

```log
# kubectl describe pod test
 Warning  Failed     49m                  kubelet            Error: failed to generate container "ddcc1d587faca0a37bc7ee0bf46abbf7ce009c31a838f00f7a2a640667b713da" spec: failed to generate spec: failed to mkdir "/var/lib/kubelet/pods/ed5ba81a-2777-4ac9-a986-33238d803bdf/volume-subpaths/config/demo/0": mkdir /var/lib/kubelet/pods/ed5ba81a-2777-4ac9-a986-33238d803bdf/volume-subpaths/config/demo/0: file exists
```

title: Inconsistent cgroup placement and naming between containerd and CRI-O with user namespaces
body:
### What happened?

When running Kubernetes with user namespaces enabled, there is an inconsistency in cgroup hierarchy and naming convention between containerd and CRI-O.

## Containerd behavior (using user namespace)
 * **Sandbox cgroup** is created inside `kubepods.slice`
 * **Container cgroup** is placed under `system.slice` instead of `kubepods.slice`, using a non-standard format that includes `slice:cri-containerd:<container_id>`
```bash
/sys/fs/cgroup/
├── kubepods.slice
│   ├── kubepods-besteffort.slice
│   │   └── kubepods-besteffort-pod<pod_id>.slice 
│   │       └── cri-containerd-<sandbox_id>.scope
│   ...
├── system.slice
│   ├── kubepods-besteffort-pod<pod_id>.slice:cri-containerd:<continer_id>
```

## Containerd behavior (without user namespace)
```bash
/sys/fs/cgroup/
├── kubepods.slice
│   ├── kubepods-besteffort.slice
│   │   └── kubepods-besteffort-pod<pod_id>.slice 
│   │       ├── cri-containerd-<sandbox_id>.scope
│   │       └── cri-containerd-<continer_id>.scope
```

It looks inconsistent because:
 * Cgroup of container that use user namespaces should be inside `kubepods.slice` just like the sandbox.
 * Naming convention is different depending on the use of userns.

## CRI-O behavior (with and without user namespaces)
 * Container and sandbox cgroups are always placed in the same location and follow a consistent naming format, whether user namespaces are enabled or not.
```bash
/sys/fs/cgroup/
├── kubepods.slice
│   ├── kubepods-besteffort.slice
│   │   ├── kubepods-besteffort-pod<pod_id>.slice
│   │   │   ├── crio-<sandbox_id>
│   │   │   └── crio-<container_id>.scope
│   │   │       └── container
├── system.slice
│   ├── crio-conmon-<container_id>.scope
```









### What did you expect to happen?

Both container runtimes should follow **consistent cgroup hierarchy and naming rules:**

 * Container cgroups should be placed inside `kubepods.slice`, not `system.slice` (as containerd currently does).

 * **Naming should follow a predictable format**, rather than using `slice:cri-containerd:<container_id>`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Enable user namespaces [Use a User Namespace With a Pod](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/user-namespaces/).
2. Deploy a pod on both container runtimes (containerd and CRI-O).
3. Compare the resulting cgroup hierarchy under: `/sys/fs/cgroup/`

### Anything else we need to know?

title: Scheduling problem after upgrade: Pods are created, Containers pending indefinitely
body:
I have made a simple patch upgrade from 1.31.4 to 1.31.7, as well as patch upgrades to Containerd, Cuda and drivers & container toolkit.

The cluster is comprised of seven nodes: 1 control plane, 2 storage servers and 4 workers with A100 GPUs.

Now all of a sudden, I have a very strange situation when scheduling nodes on the workers (only on them, others work fine). If a pod is scheduled, it will start normally on one node, but on all others it will merely be created, but never gets any containers, no events, nothing for hours.

Now I noticed that while the pod is pending, I just need to restart the kubelet on the node it is pending on and its containers will be created and it will start up fine.

hi @dasantonym. Based on the information you provided, it seems that the issue is occurring during the kubelet's process of starting the Pod, rather than being a kube-scheduler issue.

Here is a simple troubleshooting process for a Pending Pod, which may be helpful to you:
A Pending Pod may either be in the process of being scheduled or has already been scheduled, with the kubelet preparing to start it on a node.
You can distinguish between these two cases by checking whether the `nodeName` field is set.

Run the following command to check if the Pod has been assigned a `nodeName`:

```bash
kubectl get pod -o wide
NAME                    READY   STATUS      RESTARTS   AGE     IP             NODE        NOMINATED NODE   READINESS GATES
pod-1                   0/1     Pending     0          2s      <none>         <none>      <none>           <none>
pod-2                   0/1     Pending     0          9d      <none>         12.0.0.78   <none>           <none>
```
- `pod-1`: The NODE field is empty, meaning the Pod has not yet been scheduled to a node. Check the kube-scheduler logs (log level --v=5).
 - `pod-2`: The NODE field is not empty, meaning the Pod has already been scheduled to a node. Check the kubelet logs on the worker node (log level --v=5).

BTW, before fixing the issue, we need to understand the reproduction steps.

Hi @dasantonym , thank you for the logs. I have some findings:

Same issue: #117435

In kubelet, each Add Pod operation runs in a single-threaded manner (let's call it the `SyncLoopIteration goroutine`). This goroutine calls [canAdmitPod](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/73f54b67b29d77601b0bd42ad8b4992925b9df47/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2397), which checks whether there are enough resources to run the Pod. Ideally, this goroutine should not be blocked.

However, during the canAdmitPod process, when it reaches the `deviceManager`, it makes a gRPC call to an external device plugin. This gRPC call has no timeout, meaning it can block indefinitely.

If you have questions or suggestions related to my behavior, please file an issue against the [kubernetes-sigs/prow](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/prow/issues/new?title=Prow%20issue:) repository.
</details>
The error we encountered indicates that the `ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding` is missing the `parameterNotFoundAction` field.
`parameterNotFoundAction` field specifies what action should be taken if the parameter resource referenced in `paramRef` is not found.
In this case we need to add the `parameterNotFoundAction` field to the `paramRef` section of your `ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding`.

The possible updated yaml file should be:

```yaml
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding
metadata:
  name: test-policy-binding
spec:
  policyName: test-policy
  paramRef:
    name: test-config
    parameterNotFoundAction: Fail or Ignore 
  validationActions:
  - Warn

`parameterNotFoundAction` field can have two values:

- `Ignore:` Ignore the policy if the parameter is not found.
- `Fail:` Fail the policy if the parameter is not found.

We can choose either of them as per our requirement.
/sig api-machinery

Ah, thanks for the clarification. I was interpreting the error message wrong and thought I was missing another parameter or something like that. But now it makes sense.

This property however is not documented anywhere as far as I can tell. The [Validating Admission Policy Documentation page](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/validating-admission-policy/) does not even mention the `parameterNotFooundAction` and a search also does not yield any results.

---

> `parameterNotFoundAction` field can have two values:
> 
> * `Ignore:` Ignore the policy if the parameter is not found.
> * `Fail:` Fail the policy if the parameter is not found.
> 
> 
> We can choose either of them as per our requirement.

This is not true. Applying a binding with `spec.paramRef.parameterNotFoundAction: fail` results in the following error message: `The ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding "test-policy-binding" is invalid: spec.paramRef.parameterNotFoundAction: Unsupported value: "fail": supported values: "Deny", "Allow"`

The allowed values therefore are `Deny` and `Allow`.
Now fixed/documented with https://github.com/kubernetes/website/pull/48734

title: CVE-2025-1767: GitRepo Volume Inadvertent Local Repository Access
body:
**Issue Details**
A security vulnerability was discovered in Kubernetes that could allow a user with create pod permission to exploit gitRepo volumes to access local git repositories belonging to other pods on the same node.
This issue has been rated Medium ([CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1#CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N)) (score: 6.5), and assigned CVE-2025-1767.

**Am I vulnerable?**

This CVE only affects Kubernetes clusters that utilize the in-tree gitRepo volume to clone git repositories from other pods within the same node. Since the in-tree gitRepo volume feature has been deprecated and will not receive security updates upstream, any cluster still using this feature remains vulnerable. 
Affected Components
kubelet

**Affected Versions**
All versions of Kubernetes

**How do I mitigate this vulnerability?**

To mitigate this vulnerability, you must use an init container to perform git clone operation and then mount the directory into the Pod's container. An example of this approach is provided [here](https://gist.github.com/tallclair/849601a16cebeee581ef2be50c351841).

Note: You can also restrict the use of gitRepo volumes in your cluster using policies such as ValidatingAdmissionPolicy or through Restricted pod security standard policy. You can use the following Common Expression Language (CEL) expression as part of a policy to reject use of gitRepo volumes: `has(object.spec.volumes) || !object.spec.volumes.exists(v, has(v.gitRepo))`

**Detection**

To detect whether this vulnerability has been exploited, you can use the following command to list all pods that use the in-tree gitRepo volume and clones to a .git subdirectory. 
`kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.volumes[].gitRepo.repository | test("^/")) | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, repository: (.spec.volumes[] | select(.gitRepo) | .gitRepo.repository)}'`

If you find evidence that this vulnerability has been exploited, please contact [security@kubernetes.io](mailto:security@kubernetes.io) 

**Acknowledgements**
This vulnerability was reported by Christophe Hauquiert.

title: Kubernetes OIDC requires authentication for well-known and JWKS endpoints, contrary to OIDC Specification
body:
### What happened?

Kubernetes' OIDC authentication mechanism enforces authentication when querying the OIDC provider’s /.well-known/openid-configuration and JWKS (/keys) endpoints. This behavior contradicts the OIDC specification, which states that these endpoints must be publicly accessible.

The primary issue is that many services supporting resource server authentication (such as RabbitMQ and OpenSearch) rely on OIDC token validation but fail to work with Kubernetes OIDC due to the enforced authentication on these endpoints. These services expect to fetch the discovery and public keys without authentication, as per the OIDC spec, but Kubernetes' behavior prevents this, breaking compatibility with standard OIDC validation flows.

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubernetes should allow unauthenticated access to these endpoints, as OIDC-compliant providers may not require authentication for retrieving discovery (/.well-known/openid-configuration) and signing keys (/keys).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. GET https://api.k8s,example:6443/.well-known/openid-configuration

title: CRI and networking behavior
body:
### What happened?

This is a follow up to [this Slack thread](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C09QYUH5W/p1740368655309169). I can't say that I understand why, but I'm told this behavior is unexpected: the container runtime sometimes gets a `RunPodSandboxRequest` where the host port is zero.

### What did you expect to happen?

I believe @aojea wants to "check if we are sending that info on purpose through the CRI API or is just an oversight".

I think more importantly, the CRI is a bit under-documented here. The [documentation of `host_port`](https://github.com/kubernetes/cri-api/blob/v0.32.2/pkg/apis/runtime/v1/api.proto#L204) is just `Port number on the host. Default: 0 (not specified)`, which reveals basically nothing about how an implementation might handle a zero value for that field.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

This can be reproduced with minikube, Istio, and the Gateway API. It can probably be reproduced in other ways, too, but this is the most straightforward I came up with:

```bash
cd minikube  # https://github.com/kubernetes/minikube
git checkout v1.35.0
# Apply this 1-line patch so we can see `PodConfig` in the logs:
git apply patch
make local-kicbase-debug && make

# The problem can be illustrated most easily by booting up Istio and using the Gateway API
# (not sure why), but I was also observing host_port = 0 for my application pods.
./out/minikube start --container-runtime=containerd --memory=16384 --cpus=4
istioctl install --set profile=ambient --skip-confirmation
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/download/v1.2.0/standard-install.yaml
```

Where `patch` is this:

```diff
diff --git a/deploy/kicbase/containerd.toml b/deploy/kicbase/containerd.toml
index 873cee549..8bc7bf048 100644
--- a/deploy/kicbase/containerd.toml
+++ b/deploy/kicbase/containerd.toml
@@ -15,7 +15,7 @@ oom_score = 0
   address = ""
   uid = 0
   gid = 0
-  level = ""
+  level = "debug"

 [metrics]
   address = ""
```

Once you run the above, you can check the log by running:

```bash
docker exec -it minikube journalctl -u containerd | grep 'Sandbox config' | grep HostPort
```

You can see that a bunch of pods are run with a port mapping where `HostPort` is zero.

For reference, some detail of the process from one of my [presentations about kubernetes networking](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/14xNjy9ej8kGLkmSC7RsDO9-039vrwmf6sMofVOkqcD8/edit?usp=sharing)

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/fade9f97-56ab-47ae-8e22-ea4907a1da91)

This is the method that calls the runtime from kubelet

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a18b4a8d97151a25c4d8088839d77e6ba482cac3/staging/src/k8s.io/cri-client/pkg/remote_runtime.go#L190-L205

That is called from 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a18b4a8d97151a25c4d8088839d77e6ba482cac3/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_sandbox.go#L40-L42

The Pod config is generated here

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a18b4a8d97151a25c4d8088839d77e6ba482cac3/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_sandbox.go#L80

and port maps are added here to the config we send to the runtimes

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a18b4a8d97151a25c4d8088839d77e6ba482cac3/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_sandbox.go#L117-L137

No place take into consideration that the HostPort is zero

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a18b4a8d97151a25c4d8088839d77e6ba482cac3/pkg/kubelet/container/helpers.go#L359-L395

So, this confirms we send to the CRI all the container ports information, but it seems we don't tell them what they are supposed to do if hostPort is zero

At first sight it seems a very impactful to stop sending the information:
- we must understand how CRIO (@mrunalp ) and Containerd (@MikeZappa87 ) are interpreting this information
- is there any other intention for these fields than implementing HostPorts on containers ( @thockin  may remember)
of course host port zero is invalid.. typically used by client tools to request an unused port number ...

Ok, cri-o also filters hostPort 0

https://github.com/cri-o/cri-o/blob/5991aec3baf922445791cb6dbb9ed4522e251c16/server/sandbox_run.go#L73-L88

I think now is safe to say that container runtimes should not do anything if hostPort <= 0, so we need to update the API docs

Do we feel we should also filter them in the kubelet side?
I think is better to leave it as is today, there is more information related to container ports there and since this was this way for so long, based on [Hyrum's Law](https://www.hyrumslaw.com/) someone may depend on it these days

I think it would be an api decision if they want to support dynamically assigning a port number each time.. and adding that dynamically assigned port to the port mappings.. but that would require some way to get an assignment and have it mapped through.. maybe an NRI plugin.

nod on the backwards compat versioning issues.. This is the way we deal with it today.. we ignore it. I'd bet if you look through you'll see we ignore it to maintain backwards compatibility with old specs..

Agree - 0 must be interpreted as "none" and not "dynamic".  Realisitically, this should never have been sent to CRI if the value is 0 ("not specified") but it was.  We don't have any real plans for randomly-allocated hostports, but if we did it would need to be something other than "hostPort = 0"
So waht is the AI for this issue and who is on it?

Talked about this in the SIG Network meeting:

Originally it should have been an optional field (e.g. pointer in Go), but at this point we can't change that without breaking things. The expectation from hereon is that you have to "ignore 0".

title: Service account token refresh failure in pods with pvcs in terminating state
body:
### What happened?

When a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) enters the Terminating state due to a deletion request, any pod mounting this PVC experiences a failure in ServiceAccount token refresh operations. This prevents the pod from receiving updated tokens once the current token expires.

### What did you expect to happen?

Token should be refreshed because pod is running.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Set up latest kubernetes cluster (i used [kind](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/docs/user/quick-start/))
```
$ k get nodes
NAME                 STATUS   ROLES           AGE     VERSION
kind-control-plane   Ready    control-plane   5h29m   v1.32.2
```

2. Create pod mounting pvc with SA token
```
# token-test.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: simple-token-sa
  namespace: default
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: client-data-pvc
  namespace: default
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: token-client
spec:
  serviceAccountName: simple-token-sa
  containers:
  - name: client
    image: curlimages/curl:latest
    command:
      - sleep
      - infinite
    volumeMounts:
    - name: token-volume
      mountPath: /var/run/secrets/tokens
    - name: data-volume
      mountPath: /data
  volumes:
  - name: token-volume
    projected:
      sources:
      - serviceAccountToken:
          path: custom-token
          expirationSeconds: 600
          audience: my-custom-audience
  - name: data-volume
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: client-data-pvc
```
```
$ k apply -f  token-test.yaml
```

3. Request pvc deletion and the pvc enters terminating state because a pod is still mounting it.
```
$ k delete pvc client-data-pvc 
persistentvolumeclaim "client-data-pvc" deleted
```

4. Check if the token refreshes correctly before reaching its expiration time.
```
# monitor-token.sh
#!/bin/bash

# Colors for output formatting
GREEN='\033[0;32m'
YELLOW='\033[0;33m'
CYAN='\033[0;36m'
NC='\033[0m' # No Color

echo -e "${CYAN}Token Renewal Monitoring Script${NC}"
echo -e "${CYAN}------------------------------${NC}"
echo -e "Checking for token updates every 30 seconds...\n"

# Initialize variables to track changes
previous_exp=""
first_run=true

while true; do
  # Get the current timestamp for logging
  current_time=$(date "+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
  
  # Execute the command to get the token payload
  token_payload=$(kubectl exec -it token-client -- sh -c 'TOKEN=$(cat /var/run/secrets/tokens/custom-token); echo $TOKEN | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d' 2>/dev/null)
  
  # Check if command was successful
  if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
    echo -e "${YELLOW}[${current_time}] Error: Could not retrieve token. Check if the pod is running.${NC}"
    sleep 30
    continue
  fi
  
  # Extract expiration time
  exp_value=$(echo $token_payload | grep -o '"exp":[0-9]*' | cut -d':' -f2)
  
  # Format expiration time as human-readable
  exp_human=$(date -d "@$exp_value" "+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
  
  # Calculate time until expiration
  now_seconds=$(date +%s)
  seconds_remaining=$((exp_value - now_seconds))
  minutes_remaining=$((seconds_remaining / 60))
  seconds_remainder=$((seconds_remaining % 60))
  
  # If first run, just display the token info
  if $first_run; then
    echo -e "${CYAN}[${current_time}] Initial token detected${NC}"
    echo -e "Token audience: $(echo $token_payload | grep -o '"aud":\[[^]]*\]' | sed 's/"aud":\["\(.*\)"\]/\1/')"
    echo -e "Service account: $(echo $token_payload | grep -o '"sub":"[^"]*"' | sed 's/"sub":"\(.*\)"/\1/')"
    echo -e "Expires at: ${exp_human} (in ${minutes_remaining}m ${seconds_remainder}s)"
    echo -e "JWT ID: $(echo $token_payload | grep -o '"jti":"[^"]*"' | sed 's/"jti":"\(.*\)"/\1/')"
    echo -e "${CYAN}------------------------------${NC}\n"
    previous_exp=$exp_value
    first_run=false
  else
    # Check if token has been renewed (expiration time changed)
    if [ "$previous_exp" != "$exp_value" ]; then
      echo -e "${GREEN}[${current_time}] Token renewed!${NC}"
      echo -e "New expiration: ${exp_human} (in ${minutes_remaining}m ${seconds_remainder}s)"
      echo -e "New JWT ID: $(echo $token_payload | grep -o '"jti":"[^"]*"' | sed 's/"jti":"\(.*\)"/\1/')"
      echo -e "${CYAN}------------------------------${NC}\n"
      previous_exp=$exp_value
    else
      echo -e "[${current_time}] Token unchanged. Expires in ${minutes_remaining}m ${seconds_remainder}s"
    fi
  fi
  
  # Wait for 30 seconds before checking again
  sleep 30
done
```

title: CEL,CRD: Combining nested macros and CIDR containing another CIDR checks doesnt seem to work
body:
### What happened?

Hi, I trying to use CEL validation on a CRD to verify a given subnet from one field is in range of subnets of another field, but it doesnt seem to work. Please see bellow details: 

The CRD has the following fields
```
subnets:
  description: ...
  items:
    maxLength: 43
    type: string
    x-kubernetes-validations:
    - message: CIDR is invalid
      rule: isCIDR(self)
  maxItems: 2
  minItems: 1
  type: array
  x-kubernetes-validations:
  - message: When 2 CIDRs are set, they must be from different
      IP families
    rule: size(self) != 2 || !isCIDR(self[0]) || !isCIDR(self[1])
      || cidr(self[0]).ip().family() != cidr(self[1]).ip().family()
excludeSubnets:
  description: ...
  items:
    maxLength: 43
    type: string
    x-kubernetes-validations:
    - message: CIDR is invalid
      rule: isCIDR(self)
  maxItems: 25
  minItems: 1
  type: array
```

Using the following rule, to verify each item in `excludeSubnets` is in range of at least one item in `subents`:
```
self.excludeSubnets.all(e, self.subnets.exists(s,cidr(s).containsCIDR(cidr(e))))
```
1. Given the following input the validation should block the request (return false): 
```
subnets: ["192.168.0.0/16"]
excludeSubnets: ["192.200.0.0/30", "192.300.0.1/32"]
```
2. Given the following input the validation should pass (return true): 
```
subnets: ["192.168.0.0/16"]
excludeSubnets: ["192.168.0.100/32", "192.168.0.1/32"]
```
The rule doesnt seem to work and result in blocking inputs (i.e.: return false in both cases).




### What did you expect to happen?

I expect the above CEL rule to work, it should return false for input (1), and return true for input (2).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Install the following CRD  [crd.md](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/18981991/crd.md)
Apply [cudn-should-fail.md](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/18985446/cudn-should-fail.md), expect failure.
Apply [cudn-should-pass.md](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/18981992/cudn-should-pass.md), expect success.

### Anything else we need to know?

It seem that nested macros work with more simple condition, please see this [CEL playground example](https://playcel.undistro.io/?content=H4sIAAAAAAAAA3WS22rCQBCGX2WaXqgQDy30RnojRWiLbaVSpJCbMRnjwmY37OxqpPTdOxsDYkECYTKH%2F%2FtnNz9JTjqZJuMxrEnntiLwFvyO4Gm%2BgKXGY%2BlsMMVNZqTlMgeKAQ0o48lh7tWeRGMzY6Zqo49Q2wM5KoDMXjlrKjI%2BalNTa%2BtIJosYk1Nt5aD87sS1VWUNzJvaEbOScIGmDFgS9IU%2FGEUnrZshrJ3yBEcbXGuNzjM7QXdNX0ytMDpCkFKMWRUEW%2BvEfB08FOgxlRi%2BZ28LkPTr6uM91iv0ncoyKkPvM5heu8UedcArcCxRGfYt6QzohObd%2FnEut1qTnJzM2K0oYFVr4s4Y18phrGXyUJPrUNAqbAx5HqHWfUqBu09qFHvucwoEj8AwGGQmSZNIfYl8ueBbeJYjiVd26erK1qMI7eSnmRnC3WTy30Wbf5icqvF9H3uEW9mCBBn%2FrN8%2FNsGsyWECAAA%3D)

I've set up an example of this in the openshift API examples (we use this to test patterns), and as far as I can tell this does work, see the way I've implemented this here https://github.com/openshift/api/pull/2213

It's largely the same as your description but I had to change the `self.excludeSubnets.all(e, self.subnets.exists(s,cidr(s).containsCIDR(cidr(e))))` rule slightly to account for when `excludeSubnets` is not present

On further discussion, it appears that there's a bug here

The CIDR check works correctly when the IP addresses are the same (`192.168.0.0/16` will contain `192.168.0.0/24`) but when the IP addresses are not equal, this doesn't work. The part of the code that's supposed to mask the address based on the number of bits, doesn't actually do what was intended.

/cc @cici37 can you take a look? Thanks!

/triage accepted
Thank you so much for the quick fix!

nodes.title: Fix implementation of ContainsCIDR to allow non-equal addresses
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The implementation of `containsCIDR` was supposed to compare masked IP addresses. If the second IP address is masked to the same number of bits as the first, and they are equal, then the second IP address must be within the first subnet, assuming the subnet prefix length is less or equal.

The second half of the assertion for `equalMasked` was not actually masking the address, and therefore if the IPs weren't exactly equal, we would reject otherwise valid CIDR inclusions.

Eg

```
cidr('192.168.0.0/16').containsCIDR('192.168.0.0/32') <- This works today
cidr('192.168.0.0/16').containsCIDR('192.168.0.1/32') <- This does not work today
```

Once the addresses are correctly masked, the logic works as intended.

title: Generate UID for users where UID missing
body:
### What happened?


[AdmissionRequest](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/config-api/apiserver-admission.v1/#admission-k8s-io-v1-AdmissionRequest) includes [UserInfo](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/v1.32/#userinfo-v1-authentication-k8s-io) to identify which user send the request.

Use `uid` in `UserInfo` is the best way to distinguish users, but I found some authentication miss uid in the UserInfo, not limited to:
- [tokenfile](
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/authentication/token/tokenfile/tokenfile.go#L93)
- [bootstrap](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/plugin/pkg/auth/authenticator/token/bootstrap/bootstrap.go#L145)
- [oidc](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/plugin/pkg/authenticator/token/oidc/oidc.go#L804)

A empty `uid` looks really weird.



### What did you expect to happen?


I expected a UID to be populated by all authenticator, if the inputs miss uid, we should generate unique one rather than leave it as empty string.

I would like to implement it if possible.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Just check the code.

### Anything else we need to know?

From the perspective of database design, an object should always have its id.

Because it is only for authn. And in some codes, the UID is not be passed.

In most cases, this design works.

title: Excessive conntrack cleanup causes high memory (12GB) and CPU usage when any Pod with a UDP port changes
body:
### What happened? We are encountering a severe performance issue in kube-proxy (v1.32) when any Pod with a UDP port is updated (e.g., CoreDNS). In the new kube-proxy implementation, changes to Services or Pods that expose UDP ports trigger a full conntrack cleanup. This cleanup process iterates over the entire conntrack table, leading to extremely high resource consumption—sometimes up to 12 GB of memory and 1.5 CPU cores per kube-proxy instance. In a simple test, we observed 2,780 instances of the log message "Adding conntrack filter for cleanup", which caused an OOM when kube-proxy was limited to 256 MB of memory. Without that limit, kube-proxy memory usage spiked to 12 GB. On nodes with large conntrack tables, kube-proxy effectively becomes stuck, consuming all available memory each time there is a UDP endpoint change. This issue appears to be systemic; every change in a Pod with a UDP port triggers all kube-proxy instances to perform the extensive cleanup. Currently, there is no option to disable or throttle this behavior, which disrupts cluster stability and can lead to service degradation or outages. We request that the cleanup logic be revised to target only the relevant conntrack entries or that a mechanism be provided to disable or limit this aggressive cleanup behavior. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/127318 https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/126130 ### What did you expect to happen? We expected kube-proxy to handle conntrack cleanup in a more efficient and targeted way. Even if it needs to scan a significant portion of the conntrack table, it should do so without causing a spike to 12 GB of memory usage. Ideally, it would either: - Limit its cleanup to entries relevant to the specific changed UDP endpoint. - Provide a way to configure or disable this aggressive cleanup process so it does not risk out-of-memory (OOM) events or excessively high CPU usage. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? - Deploy multiple Pods that generate a high volume of DNS requests, for example: - A simple Golang application making repeated DNS lookups without any caching mechanism. - Observe kube-proxy resource usage (memory and CPU) on that node. - Delete or update the coredns Pod (which also uses UDP DNS). - Watch the logs and resource usage of kube-proxy closely, noting the surge in memory (potentially up to 12 GB) and CPU usage as it performs the conntrack cleanup. ### Anything else we need to know? ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f75f0bc0-e394-45fa-b323-2f6fc0570386) ### Kubernetes version
```console $ kubectl version Client Version: v1.31.2 Kustomize Version: v5.4.2 Server Version: v1.32.0-eks-5ca49cb ```
### Cloud provider
AWS
### OS version
```console # On Linux: Amazon Linux 2 5.10.230-223.885.amzn2.aarch64 ```
### Install tools
EKS
### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)
containerd://1.7.23
### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)
kube-proxy:v1.32.0-minimal-eksbuild.2

I can think of three ways to figure out if a conntrack flow is owned by kube-proxy:

[1] seems a straight forward way [2] and [3] may required API changes.

Increasing the `--iptables-min-sync-period duration` will alleviate the problem, since the reconciler will run every that period.

The problem is that we were not checking the Service Ports on the conntrack entries, hence any UDP traffic associated to a Service IP was deleted, and since overlays CNIs like flannel use to use UDP for traffic (vxlan), any new inter node traffic will create new entries that will be deleted again, it was easy to reproduce even with an unit test  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130484#discussion_r1976011944 . This also explains this comment https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/129982#issuecomment-2639495058,   that was puzzling me, how is possible we were matching so many stale entries on the conntrack reconciler filters.

The backport of the fix landed in 1.32.3 https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/b0554e32c769fe68eb2bd770134bbb03b9a41eea .

nodes.title: conntrack reconciler must check the dst port
nodes.body:
/kind bug
/kind regression

Fixes #129982

Services can expose applications on a tuple IP:Port, where IP can be ClusterIP|ExternalP|LoadBalancerIP:ServicePort or *:NodePort. We also have the list of IPs with the backends associated.

When implementing a reconcilation loop for conntrack we have a list of this tuples, we match the conntrack entries that match the frontend tuple IP:Port or *:NodePort and we removes the entries that does not have a known endpoints.

However, during the implementation we forget to check for the ServicePort, causing that the reconciler got busy with any IP on a Service that had a large amount of UDP entries , specially problematic on Services with ExternalIPs and use overlay, since those use UDP for encapsulation extensevely.


```release-note
Fixes a 1.32 regression kube-proxy, when using a Service with External or LoadBalancer IPs on UDP services , was consuming a large amount of CPU because it was not filtering by the Service destination port and trying to delete all the UDP entries associated to the service.
```

title: Service with selector does not create all required endpoints, when a POD has multiple containers with a matching named port.
body:
### What happened?

I have a Deployment which creates POD's containing two containers, each container has a named port "grpc-service" on a different port to avoid conflicts.  I want a k8s service to connect to these grpc services in a round-robin fashion and also be able to use the k8s API to retrieve the list of endpoints.  I attempt to do this by creating a simple service, with a label selector that matches the container, and names the target-port.  However when I scale the  deployment only one of the containers is matched to the service,  I was expecting both containers to be matched resulting in two endpoints for each POD instance.

The generated endpoint looks like this, when the deployment is scaled to two replica's (I've trimmed out the targetRef's to keep it brief):

```

We have a number of different containers, all providing many different rpc's via gRPC.  However the containers also all have a small common set of rpc's for monitoring status and metrics etc of that container instance.  Its seems a waste to have many ports open for each rpc within a container, so we have one gRPC Server running in each container serving all the rpc's implemented within that container.  Also some of our POD's are required to have multiple containers.

We therefore wish to have a service which maps onto all the gRPC Server ports of any POD with a matching label and port name, regardless of how many containers are in any pod.

I see, you want a wildcard for portnames , right?

@thockin you may have interesting alternatives or suggestions here

The fact that we allow same-name ports in different containers is a bug that we cannot fix (because of compat).  I thought we had merged a warning for that, but maybe I lost track of it?

As you have seen, we do not have a way to model what you are describing.  There's an assumption of fungibility between endpoints behind a given service+port, which it sounds like you'd be violating?  IIUC...

What I mean is that you have 2 containers in a pod with the same schema, but they are not serving the same data, right?

That's correct they are non-fungable and that's because the containers are stateful.  The state is described by the same schema, but the actual values will be different depending on the application lifecycle of a particular container instance.  We have a frontend (Web App) that needs to display the application status of each container.  Hence each container implements a gRPC rpc service to provide that status information.   So I was expecting a Service would be the ideal solution, the frontend simply needs to get a list of the endpoints for the service and call each in-turn in-order to get the status information to display.  This already works fine when there is only one container in a POD, but fails when there are multiple containers in the POD (as only the first container is considered),

A similar service might be required if we wanted to expose the Java JMX management MBean Server within our containers for inspection during development via another web app.

Given that an endpoint is a combination of an IP Address with Port Number, I don't understand why having more than one in a POD is any different to having them split across different PODs?  I did try creating the endpoints with two subsets, as described above and it was accepted by the k8s API, but the routing did not change, I guess because I manually made the change, instead of the controller doing.

The current documentation at https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/ doesn't seem to mention the endpoints have to be fungible and suggests that a label selector to match the pods and targetPort Name will match all the endpoints.

So without this capability I suppose we would need one service per container, which would mean the services would have to be created dynamically as the Deployments were scaled up or down.  The frontend application would then have to find these services.  Having to do this would seem to defeat the main benefit of the service model that finds the endpoints!

Only having one container per pod would seem like a possible solution, but due to reasons beyond my control, I'm required to have multiple containers per POD in some instances!

The assumption of fungibility is sort of baked into the service load-balancing model - you have to know which port you want when you access a cluster IP, and you don't get to choose which pod that routes to.  If that's not fungible, what does it mean?

We do support headless services, which becomes more of a discoverable thing, but the most common exposure mechanism - DNS - also assumes fungibility for a given SRV or A query. 

I think I get what you are trying to do, and it's not even really wrong, per se, it's just not something we support today.  All of the logic we have is around the common use-case, and as I mentioned, the fact that you are allowed to have multiple ports of the same name is basically a bug.

I wouldn't be against trying to support this, but I can't say off the top of my head how it should look - it breaks fungibility so most of the service-oriented functionality is moot.  It would be a fairly substantial proposal, just thinking about all the places that need to be adapted to this. 

We have published some logic for writing custom endpoint slice controllers, so that might be a vector for you to at least collect the information you want to collect?

title: Compressed pod log files default to 644 permissions
body:

title: "Error syncing pod, skipping" err="rpc error: code = Unavailable desc = connection error: desc = \"transport: Error while dialing: dial unix /run/containerd/containerd.sock: connect: connection refused\"" pod="" podUID=""
body:
### What happened?

Pod has been terminating, error: "Error syncing pod, skipping" err="rpc error: code = Unavailable desc = connection error: desc = \"transport: Error while dialing: dial unix /run/containerd/containerd.sock: connect: connection refused\"" pod="" podUID=""， Actually, containerd is normal

### What did you expect to happen?

Pod pulled up normally

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Dec  5 23: Upgrade caas from 53 onwards
Dec  5 23: 56 Node Restart
Dec 5 23:56:52 containerd starts after power on
Since the start of the kubelet process on Dec 6 00:00:23, it has not been restarted yet. It should be at this point in time that the kubelet was upgraded
Dec 6 00:00:06 Crittl Check the start and run time of the container process for nbidataserver (cinit process inside the container)
Dec 6 00:01:16 ps Check the startup time of the business process. The probe may not be ready for a short period of time before starting, and the kubelet may only sync after reaching certain conditions 
Dec 6 00:01:37 nbidataservice updataPodContainerResources first reported failure containerdsock connection rejected and kept reporting errors afterwards
Dec 6 00:01:38 containerd upgraded and started up until now



Latest progress: This issue is caused by enabling the InPlacePodVerticalScaling feature
Event replay:
Event 1:2024-12-24 22:41:33 Machine Power On/Off
Event 2:2024-12-24 22:47:53 kubelet starts to start, Pod starts to be pulled up
Event 3:2024-12-24 22:49:03 containerd starts
Event 4:2024-12-24 22:49:04 kubelet started pulling up smauthservice, but received an error message "server is not initialized yet" when accessing containerd. After containerd started, smauthservice started normally.
Event 5:2024-12-24 22:54:12: The upgrade of smauthservice started, and the Kubernetes control plane set the pod smauthservice to Terminating state, which has been consistent until now.
Cause analysis:
1. The kubelet caches real pod information (also known as pod cache), which is synchronized from containerd by PLEG (PodLifecycle Event Generator) coroutine timing. PLEG itself also caches the real pod state (known as PLEG cache). If PLEG detects a difference between the real container state and its own cache, it will synchronize the real pod information to the pod cache.
2. After enabling the InPlacePodVerticalScaling feature, during the pod startup phase, if the pod is expanding, kubelet will query the real pod status from containerd and update the pod cache directly without PLEG. At this time, because containerd cannot access it, unknown status will be saved to the pod cache (Event 4). However, PLEG will not update the pod cache again because the actual pod status is no different from its own cache.
3. Later on, when upgrading the pod, the coroutine for handling pod deletion needed to retrieve the actual pod state from the pod cache for tuning. However, an unknown state was obtained, so the deletion of the pod was stopped and the pod remained in Terminating (Event 5).


### Anything else we need to know?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/20f84b12#diff-75172373a06386d9bba8f7a8841fdeab9f8681ce68a1af56331fbc7ff41102e0R86


IMO, we should bypass `cpu` and `mempory` if pod request is zero.

cc @sanposhiho @AxeZhan @macsko 
Maybe we should first confirm whether this change is reasonable.

> IMO, we should bypass cpu and mempory if pod request is zero.

I don't think so, the logic here seems to have deliberately taken into account the CPU/memory that the node has already been requested for.

What do you mean by "return wrong score"? If nodes have different requested resources, the score should be different on different nodes, no?

What's the proposal, I mean, not from the implementation perspective, but from the behavior perspective? (i.e., what is going to change after the proposal from users' pov?)

For now, it makes sense to me to still return scores (based on already-allocated resources of nodes) for pods even with zero requests because they'll anyway use some CPU/memory once they're running. It's safer to run pods with zero requests in less busy nodes.

We ignore extended resources because, I guess, we assume Pods without the request for extended resources won't consume those resources at runtime.

> If nodes have different requested resources, the score should be different on different nodes, no?

I think the socre should be same. If the scores differ, too many pods with zero resource requests might get scheduled to the same node.

Additionally, the requested resources for the scheduled node would no longer change.

> It's safer to run pods with zero requests in less busy nodes.

the pods with zero requests will not make less busy nodes to busy, because it will not change the node requested.

> too many pods with zero resource requests might get scheduled to the same node.

I think this will not happen, the requested resources of a node will be updated with a default value if the pod has no requests.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a499facee693a1a83daadb82d88f7b51d324ffc5/pkg/scheduler/framework/types.go#L1035

> the pods with zero requests will not make less busy nodes to busy

I mean, they just don't have any allocation, but they do use cpu/memory as long as the resource limit and the node's resource capacity allows. So, if you only look at the requested resources, then the node looks not busy, but actually it's busier with Pod(s) with no request.

> too many pods with zero resource requests might get scheduled to the same node.

~~But, it's a reasonable argument, does any plugin look at the pod number at the score phase? (I'm outside now and cannot check the impl myself)
I remember, at the filter, the resource fit plugin does.~~

EDIT: I didn't look at @AxeZhan 's comment.

But, I'm wondering if it still would make sense to take the pod number into consideration at Score phase. (If we haven't yet anywhere)
Let's say the amount of requested resources on each node is the same, we probably prefer to place a new pod to a node with the fewest running pods...? (given the node has the upper limit on the num of running pods.)

> But, I'm wondering if it still would make sense to take the pod number into consideration at Score phase. (If we haven't yet anywhere)

It works in node resource plugin using `NonZeroReuqested`. 

For real `Requested`, this maybe cause too many pods scheduled to a node that running a `big pod` which request all this node resource.

> For real Requested, this maybe cause too many pods scheduled to a node that running a big pod which request all this node resource.

I know, it might be not ideal in some scenarios, but, in the first place, users must put the resource requests if they want an ideal behavior. We cannot determine what is ideal to do with zero request pods.

---

Again, @Bowser1704 do you have your own proposal to this problem? (Or, you just wanted to open a discussion for this problem.)

If you still propose always returning a 0 score for pods with zero request, what's a counter punch for [my previous comments](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/129138#issuecomment-2531490373)?

I think what @Bowser1704 's proposal is to return same score for every node when pod has no cpu&memory request.
I'm a bit concerned about this, as it means we've lost the functionality of resource plugin with this kind pod.

I checked https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/105845 and I'm not sure why we stop using `nonZeroRequested` in  `NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation`.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/102925 says it's because too many zero requested containers can result in a huge nonZeroRequest and thus influence the schedule result.

Checking pod num on the nodes feels right for me. 
And besides, with https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/2837, maybe we can change the default cpu/memory value from container-level to pod-level?

As the reason described at my previous comments, I still prefer to keep the current behaviour (+ add a pod number based scoring, but probably smaller weight than cpu/mem), compared to just returning zero scores with pods with no resources. 
If there're node-a with no running pod, node-b with a small pod, and node-c with a huge pod, it makes sense to schedule a pod onto node-a, even if the request is zero, because the pod will anyway consume some resources.
/cc @alculquicondor @macsko @dom4ha

For now my proposol is just make NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation plugin `useRequest` to be configurable.



> I know, it might be not ideal in some scenarios, but, in the first place, users must put the resource requests if they want an ideal behavior. We cannot determine what is ideal to do with zero request pods.


Got that. I think it's just a tradeoff. 

Return same score means it will use the reservoir sampling, so all feasible nodes are fair, but it might schedule pod to `really busy` nodes.

Use pod-number score is ok, but there's still a potential to schedule too many zero-resource-request pods onto a node which has huge pod.

> I checked https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/105845 and I'm not sure why we stop using nonZeroRequested in NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/102925 says it's because too many zero requested containers can result in a huge nonZeroRequest and thus influence the schedule result.

@AxeZhan I test NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation with `nonZeroRequested`, the requested (for cpu and memory) maybe larger than allocatable, and plugin will return score `100` for the `overflow` node. see code below:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8a39b6062060ffb4fba52f53c011bd00428db194/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/noderesources/balanced_allocation.go#L145-L147.

> Return same score means it will use the reservoir sampling, so all feasible nodes are fair, but it might schedule pod to really busy nodes.

All the feasible nodes are selected truly randomly. (assuming pods with zero request don't get affected by any other scoring decision) But it doesn't mean all pods with zero requests would be spread to all nodes fairly. That depends on the scheduling order. All zero-request pods may go to one very-busy node, unluckily (extreme example).

Another thought: what if we calculate scores for pods with zero requests completely separately so that they would get spread to all nodes equally? So, all nodes would get the burden coming from pods with zero request truly equally.
It might be simpler/safer than adding a pod-number based scoring, which has a broader blast radius.

> All the feasible nodes are selected truly randomly. 

Every feasible node probability is 1/cntOfMaxScore if node score is same. see code below:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8a39b6062060ffb4fba52f53c011bd00428db194/pkg/scheduler/schedule_one.go#L893-L899

Yes, and that means all pods with the same score could select the same node, if you're unlucky.

---

At a high level, there are two options right now:

- Keep the current resource-based scoring even for zero-request pods basically, but try to avoid scheduling too many zero-request pods onto the same node somehow.
  - maybe a pod-number based scoring or maybe bring back a pod default request. (But, looks like both are not perfect?)
- Try to spread zero-request pods equally.
  - It's essentially similar to what @Bowser1704 wants to propose, from the behavior perspective, no? (If not, correct me what is your proposal _from the behavior perspective_, [like I said at the very beginning](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/129138#issuecomment-2530824028))
  - I'm suggesting, if we want to go this way, it's better to still give scores based on how each node has zero-request pods, not just returning zero score, which is too random.

/unassign

I didn't participate in the discussion later. sorry for this :)

> Yes, and that means all pods with the same score could select the same node, if you're unlucky.

IMO, this probability is too small, it's exponential growth.

> maybe a pod-number based scoring or maybe bring back a pod default request. (But, looks like both are not perfect?)

Yes, but we can use nonZeroRequested and fix NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation plugin problem above https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/129138#issuecomment-2534185206.

> Try to spread zero-request pods equally.

Yes, it's what I want to propose.

> if we want to go this way, it's better to still give scores based on how each node has zero-request pods

Agreed that.

> IMO, this probability is too small, it's exponential growth.

That depends on the scheduling order. The scheduler doesn't always schedule zero-request pods.
I know all pods go to the same node is the extreme example anyway though.

Also, there's a deletion of existing running pods, so random assigning (= returning zero score) doesn't make sense to make a good result. Anyways, on this second option, I think we're on the same page according to your last comment; we should give a score based on the existing running zero-request pods.

> we can use nonZeroRequested and fix NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation plugin problem above https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/129138#issuecomment-2534185206.

How does "return score 100 for the overflow node" make sense? It means that we keep putting pods to the overflow node, no?

> we should give a score based on the existing running zero-request pods.

Agreed that, but it maybe cost a lot to count all existing running zero-request pods.

> How does "return score 100 for the overflow node" make sense? It means that we keep putting pods to the overflow node, no?

Yes, so we need to fix it. Maybe we can return score 0 for the overflow node.

>  it maybe cost a lot to count all existing running zero-request pods.

We do need to pay attention to the calculation cost, yes. But I believe that won't be an issue by having a cache within the nodeinfo or somewhere. 

> Maybe we can return score 0 for the overflow node.

That would bring back the behavior before https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/102925. 
How would you prevent the problem raised there and also discussed in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/105220?

> How would you prevent the problem raised there and also discussed in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/105220?

I got, it can't. It's really hard to make schedule balance with nonZeroRequested in NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation, because every node fraction of cpu to memory is different.

You are right, use nonZeroRequested is not perfect.

> But I believe that won't be an issue by having a cache within the nodeinfo or somewhere.

Agreed that.
Yeah, so we'd need an idea to address those problems raised there, if we go with that option.

I initially thought there might be a problem with cache-ing, we've had issues in the past where failure to write to cache dir was silent, but I've tried several variants and that's working as expected, iow. we always read data from apiserver. 

> * It eventually resolved after 10 mins

That 10 mins is interesting, we bumped the timeout on cached data to 6h in kubectl long time ago (#107141). The only real difference between the two is that 1.29:
```
Accept: application/json;g=apidiscovery.k8s.io;v=v2beta1;as=APIGroupDiscoveryList,application/json
```
whereas 1.30: 
```
Accept: application/json;g=apidiscovery.k8s.io;v=v2;as=APIGroupDiscoveryList,application/json;g=apidiscovery.k8s.io;v=v2beta1;as=APIGroupDiscoveryList,application/json
```
ie. with 1.30 we prefer `apidiscovery.k8s.io/v2` over `apidiscovery.k8s.io/v2beta1`, but we'll work with both. 1.29 works only with the latter. 

What you can do is to run the following command:
```
curl -k -H "Authorization: Bearer ${token}" -H "Accept: application/json;g=apidiscovery.k8s.io;v=v2beta1;as=APIGroupDiscoveryList,application/json" https://<your_apiserver>/apis?timeout=32s
```
and compare that with the output from 
```
curl -k -H "Authorization: Bearer ${token}" -H "Accept: application/json;g=apidiscovery.k8s.io;v=v2;as=APIGroupDiscoveryList,application/json" https://<your_apiserver>/apis?timeout=32s
```
the only expected difference between the two will be `apidiscovery.k8s.io/v2beta1` vs `apidiscovery.k8s.io/v2` in `apiVersion` field. This will allow us to narrow down the problem, whether it's in the apiserver or client. 

> * Currently we tried to reproduce outside of the test environment but not yet able to simply reproduce in running in a container env, it reproduced 100% in our test environment which is running from a standard container started by docker.  Istio version is 1.21.x, which support both v1beta1 and v1alpha3.

This is telling me that it's purely coincidental, we have 3 different people trying it out and nobody can reproduce it, only that single env of yours. But like I said above, that diff on the apidiscovery can be helpful.

Hi, just run the diff of below curl 
```
curl -k -H "Authorization: Bearer ${token}" -H "Accept: application/json;g=apidiscovery.k8s.io;v=v2beta1;as=APIGroupDiscoveryList,application/json" https://<our_apiserver>/apis?timeout=32s
```
and
```
curl -k -H "Authorization: Bearer ${token}" -H "Accept: application/json;g=apidiscovery.k8s.io;v=v2;as=APIGroupDiscoveryList,application/json" https://<our_apiserver>/apis?timeout=32s
```
only difference of the output is
```
3c3
<   "apiVersion": "apidiscovery.k8s.io/v2beta1",
---
>   "apiVersion": "apidiscovery.k8s.io/v2",
```

/assign @seans3 
/triage accepted

I think I found the cause on the machine where the issue was reproducible.
The machine running kubectl had time discrepancies, with its clock running about 30 minutes behind the cluster's clock.
I suspect this affected caching, though I'm not sure why only the new API was impacted.
Once the clock was synchronized, the issue stopped being reproducible.

title: [InPlacePodVerticalScaling]kubelet sometimes set `.status.resize` incorrectly
body:
### What happened?

In cluster which enable InPlacePodVerticalScaling, If I only resize resources, I will watch `.status.resize` and `.status.containerStatuses[x].resources` to know whether the resize progress.

I have encountered some corner cases that are difficult to consistently reproduce:
1. User changes cpu request from 200m to 100m
2. Kubelet set  `.status.resize` to `InProgress`
3. Kubelet set `.status.resize` to be nil and set `.status.containerStatuses[x].resources` to be 100m
4. Kubelet set `.status.resize` to be `InProgress` and set `.status.containerStatuses[x].resources` to be 200m
5. finally,  Kubelet set `.status.resize` to be nil and set `.status.containerStatuses[x].resources` to be 100m again

### What did you expect to happen?

Under normal circumstances, steps 4 and 5 should not take place.

I have discovered some relevant information in the Kubelet logs.

title: [SidecarContainers] Failed to get proper phase after the node reboot
body:
### What happened?

If a pod has an init container with restartPolicy "Always" (sidecar), it may lose the pending phase after the node reboot and start the regular containers before initializing the init containers.

/sig node
/priority important-soon
/kind bug

This is similar to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/126650, but separated as it only affects the pod with restartable init containers.

### What did you expect to happen?

After the node reboot, the remaining pod should start from the pending phase and run the init containers one by one to initialize.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create and initialize the pod with an init container with "Always" container restart policy.
2. Restart the node.

This PR fixes the pod with restartable init containers to have a proper phase after the pod sandbox re-creation.

title: when 'hostPort' is unset from pre-existing deployment using hostNetwork, it spawns new replicaset but fails to delete pre-existing replicaset
body:
### What happened?

- i prepared an nginx container to listen on port 9033
- deployed it with a deployment that was configured to use 'hostNetwork: true' and explicitly set 'hostPort: 9033'
- i edited the deployment by simply deleting the 'hostPort' entry
- i then applied the edited deployment manifest

Hi @peterochodo ,

It seems the issue arises due to a port conflict between the pods. Initially, the deployment was configured with hostNetwork: true and hostPort: 9033, which worked as expected. However, when the hostPort was removed from the deployment configuration but hostNetwork remained enabled, a second pod was launched but got stuck in the 'Pending' state.

Here’s why:

When hostNetwork: true is set, the pod binds to the node’s network stack, and in the initial deployment, the pod successfully bound to hostIP:9033.
After removing hostPort, Kubernetes defaults to using the container port but still binds to the host IP due to hostNetwork: true. Since the first pod is already occupying port 9033 on the host, the second pod cannot bind to that same port, causing the conflict and resulting in the 'Pending' state.
To resolve this, you have two options:

Remove both hostNetwork and hostPort: This will make the pod use the cluster network instead of the host network, avoiding any port conflicts.
Use a different deployment strategy:  like "type=Recreate" instead of RollingUpdate.

Let me know if this helps or if you need further clarification.

/remove-sig scheduling
/sig apps

> [rgav-manepalli](/Bhargav-manepalli)

Thank you.

Yes, the upgrade strategy of 'RollingUpdate' is incompatible with a scenario like this whereby a hostport is monopolized by the currently running pod: The newly launched pod will get stuck in 'Pending' while it awaits for the hostport to be freed, whereas the pre-existing pod will remain running until at least 1 new pod is transitions to 'Running' state. Deadlock.

Option 2, seems appropriate for my situation. Modifying deployment.spec.strategy.type to equal 'Recreate' solved my problem.

```
# diff manifest-original.yaml manifest-mod.yaml 
13,16c13
<     rollingUpdate:
<       maxSurge: 1
<       maxUnavailable: 0
<     type: RollingUpdate
---
>     type: Recreate
28d24
<           hostPort: 9033

```

title: [Bug] Scheduler fails to schedule a pod due to a race condition
body:
### What happened?

A bug in the scheduler increases the time spent on scheduling a pod **from <1 second to 5 minutes**.

We discovered the bug when repeating the steps described in a fixed bug report [#106780](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/106780). The setting and steps are as follows:

We have 1 node with 32Gi memory, and 3 pods to schedule: 
p1 / request 10Gi memory / low-priority,
p2 / request 25Gi memory / medium-priority,
p3 / request 20Gi memory / high-priority.

We perform the following steps:
1. add `p1` and wait until `p1` is running
2. add `p2` and wait until `p1` is terminating; this is because there are not enough resources to host both pods and `p2` has a higher priority.
**Note that at this point, `p2` is not running yet.**
3. add `p3` and wait until `p3` is running; `p2` is pending because `p2` and `p3` cannot coexist on `node0`.
4. re-add `p1` and wait until `p1` is running; `p1` should be able to run since there are enough resources to host both pods: 10 + 20 < 32

Interestingly, we find that if step 4 happened immediately after step 3, then `p1` fails to get scheduled with the reason `Insufficient Memory` and eventually gets scheduled after 5 minutes. If there is some short period between step 3 and step 4 (say 2 seconds), then `p1` is scheduled properly immediately.

#### What is the root cause?

After code and log inspections (see below), we have found the root cause of this bug: it's caused by the race condition between (A) `p1` is re-added and handled by the scheduler and (B) `p2`'s `nominated_node_name` is cleared. If A happens before B, then the bug occurs.

#### Why does 2 second make the difference?

The reason is that `p2`'s `nominated_node_name` is cleared *when it (a nominated pod) is scheduled again and failed*. But as the `p2`'s first schedule failed (need to wait for preemption to finish), it's put to BackoffQueue and need to wait for a few seconds before it's put back to ActionQueue and scheduled again.

So 
1. If `p1` is added before `p2` is scheduled again (without 2s sleep), it will **fail** as `p2`'s `nomianted_node_name` is not cleared.
2. But if we add the 2s sleep, `p2` is scheduled again and its `nominated_node_name` is cleared before `p1` is added. In this case, `p1` will be **schedulable** to node0.

#### How to fix it?

1. A potential fix is:
Register all plugins that need to be aware of pods to events triggered by updates to a pod's `nominated_node_name`. This way, a failed pod will be retried as soon as any pod's `nominated_node_name` is cleared.

2. If this is too radical and can cause performance issues, another solution is: 
When a pod is bound to a node with nominated pods, either 
a) re-check the previously nominated pods (that nominated to this node), 
b) or clear the `nominated_node_name` of these nominated pods.
In this way, upcoming pods won't fail unreasonably and won't have to wait 5 minutes for the next retry.


### What did you expect to happen?

`p1` should be immediately scheduled.

  labels:

status:
  allocatable:
    cpu: "32"
    memory: "32Gi"
    pods: "110"
  capacity:
    cpu: "32"
    memory: "32Gi"
    pods: "110"
```

```yaml

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: p1
spec:

    image: nginx
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: "10Gi"

  priorityClassName: low-priority
```

  priorityClassName: medium-priority
```

kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: p3
spec:
  containers:
  - name: p3-container
    image: nginx
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: "20Gi"
  priorityClassName: high-priority
```

kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: high-priority
value: 1000000
globalDefault: false
description: "This priority class should be used for XYZ service pods only."
---

  name: medium-priority
value: 500000

description: "This priority class should be used for XYZ service pods only."
---
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1

globalDefault: false
description: "This priority class should be used for XYZ service pods only."

import time
import shutil
import logging
from time import sleep
from os import path, makedirs
from logging import getLogger
from kubernetes import config, watch
from kubernetes.client import *
from kubernetes.utils import *
from time import strftime

logger = getLogger(__name__)
config.load_kube_config()
v1 = CoreV1Api()
k8s_cli = ApiClient()


log_dir = path.dirname(__file__)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    log_path = path.join(log_dir, f"issue-106780-reproduction-{strftime('%Y-%m-%d-%H-%M-%S')}")
    shutil.rmtree(log_path, ignore_errors=True)
    makedirs(log_path, exist_ok=True)
    log_file = path.join(log_path, 'reproduce.log')

                        filemode='w',
                        filename=log_file,
                        format='%(asctime)s - %(name)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s',

    node0_yaml = path.join(path.dirname(__file__), 'node0.yaml')
    p1_yaml = path.join(path.dirname(__file__), 'p1.yaml')
    p2_yaml = path.join(path.dirname(__file__), 'p2.yaml')
    p3_yaml = path.join(path.dirname(__file__), 'p3.yaml')
    priority_class_yaml = path.join(path.dirname(__file__), 'priority_class.yaml')
    w = watch.Watch()

    # 1. create priority class
    create_from_yaml(k8s_client=k8s_cli, yaml_file=priority_class_yaml)
    logger.info(f"PriorityClass created")

    # 2. add node0
    create_from_yaml(k8s_client=k8s_cli, yaml_file=node0_yaml)
    logger.info(f"Node: node0 created")

    # 3. add p1
    create_from_yaml(k8s_client=k8s_cli, yaml_file=p1_yaml)
    logger.info(f"Pod: p1 added")

    # 3. check p1 is running
    p1_running = False
    for event in w.stream(v1.list_namespaced_pod,
                          field_selector=f'metadata.name=p1',
                          namespace="default",
                          timeout_seconds=int(5)):
        p1 = event['object']
        if event['object'].status.phase == "Running":
            p1_running = True
            logger.info(f"Pod: {p1.metadata.name} scheduled on node {p1.spec.node_name}")
            break
    assert p1_running

    # 4. add p2
    create_from_yaml(k8s_client=k8s_cli, yaml_file=p2_yaml)
    logger.info(f"Pod: p2 added")

    # 4. check p1 is terminating (by p2)
    for event in w.stream(v1.list_namespaced_pod,
                          field_selector=f'metadata.name=p1',
                          namespace="default",
                          timeout_seconds=int(3)):
        logger.info(f"Pod: {event['object'].metadata.name}, event: {event['type']}")
        logger.info(
            f"deletion_timestamp: {event['object'].metadata.deletion_timestamp}, status: {event['object'].status.phase}")
        if event['object'].metadata.deletion_timestamp is not None and event['object'].status.phase in (
        'Pending', 'Running'):
            logger.info(f"Pod: {p1.metadata.name} is terminating")
            break

    # 5. add p3 and wait for p3 running (p3 will terminate p2 / let p2 pending)
    create_from_yaml(k8s_client=k8s_cli, yaml_file=p3_yaml)
    p3_running = False
    for event in w.stream(v1.list_namespaced_pod,
                          field_selector=f'metadata.name=p3',
                          namespace="default",
                          timeout_seconds=int(5)):
        p3 = event['object']
        if p3.status.phase == "Running":
            logger.info(f"Pod: {p3.metadata.name} scheduled on node p3")
            p3_running = True
            break
    assert p3_running

    # 6. reapply and check p1 schedulable
    create_from_yaml(k8s_client=k8s_cli, yaml_file=p1_yaml)
    tic = time.time()
    logger.info(f"Pod: p1 re-applied")

    # 7. watch pod1 events and wait it to be scheduled
    p1_running = False
    for event in w.stream(v1.list_namespaced_pod,
                          field_selector=f'metadata.name=p1',
                          namespace="default",
                          timeout_seconds=int(600)):
        p1 = event['object']
        if p1.status.phase == "Running":
            p1_running = True
            logger.info(f"Pod: {p1.metadata.name} scheduled on node {p1.spec.node_name}")
            break

    if not p1_running:
        logger.error(f"Pod: {p1.metadata.name} is not scheduled in 600s")
        assert False
    else:
        logger.info(f"Pod: {p1.metadata.name}, " + f"time between add and scheduled: {time.time() - tic}")

In response to [this](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/126700):

>### What happened?
>
>A bug in the scheduler increases the time spent on scheduling a pod **from <1 second to 5 minutes**.
>
>We discovered the bug when repeating the steps described in a fixed bug report [#106780](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/106780). The setting and steps are as follows:
>
>We have 1 node with 32Gi memory, and 3 pods to schedule: 
>p1 / request 10Gi memory / low-priority,
>p2 / request 25Gi memory / medium-priority,
>p3 / request 20Gi memory / high-priority.
>
>We perform the following steps:
>1. add `p1` and wait until `p1` is running
>2. add `p2` and wait until `p1` is terminating; this is because there are not enough resources to host both pods and `p2` has a higher priority.
>**Note that at this point, `p2` is not running yet.**
>3. add `p3` and wait until `p3` is running; `p2` is pending because `p2` and `p3` cannot coexist on `node0`.
>4. re-add `p1` and wait until `p1` is running; `p1` should be able to run since there are enough resources to host both pods: 10 + 20 < 32
>
>Interestingly, we find that if step 4 happened immediately after step 3, then `p1` fails to get scheduled with the reason `Insufficient Memory` and eventually gets scheduled after 5 minutes. If there is some short period between step 3 and step 4 (say 2 seconds), then `p1` is scheduled properly immediately.
>
>#### What is the root cause?
>
>After code and log inspections (see below), we have found the root cause of this bug: it's caused by the race condition between (A) `p1` is re-added and handled by the scheduler and (B) `p2`'s `nominated_node_name` is cleared. If A happens before B, then the bug occurs.
>
>#### Why does 2 second make the difference?
>
>The reason is that `p2`'s `nominated_node_name` is cleared *when it (a nominated pod) is scheduled again and failed*. But as the `p2`'s first schedule failed (need to wait for preemption to finish), it's put to BackoffQueue and need to wait for a few seconds before it's put back to ActionQueue and scheduled again.
>
>So 
>1. If `p1` is added before `p2` is scheduled again (without 2s sleep), it will **fail** as `p2`'s `nomianted_node_name` is not cleared.
>2. But if we add the 2s sleep, `p2` is scheduled again and its `nominated_node_name` is cleared before `p1` is added. In this case, `p1` will be **schedulable** to node0.
>

>#### How to fix it?
>
>A potential fix is to register all plugins that need to be aware of pods to events triggered by updates to a pod's `nominated_node_name`. This way, a failed pod will be retried as soon as any pod's `nominated_node_name` is cleared.
>
>If this is too radical and can cause performance issues, another solution is: When a pod is bound to a node with nominated pods, either re-check the previously nominated pods (that nominated to this node) or clear the `nominated_node_name` of these nominated pods. In this way, upcoming pods won't fail unreasonably and won't have to wait 5 minutes for the next retry.

hi @scheduler-tester , I found that it is not only because of `nominated_node_name`, but also related to priority. I think it cannot be simply fixed according to 2 in how to fix. Although p1 and p2 are both nominated, if the priority of p2 is not higher than p1, p1 can still be scheduled quickly. If I fix it according to `2`, I think it will destroy some existing logic

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c999f9d828009f0a535237aca74ce2e5f6a8088c/pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/framework.go#L1035-L1045

If I comment out `nodeInfoOut.AddPodInfo(pi)`, p1 can be scheduled to node0 immediately
