@scheduler-tester ,I also found an interesting phenomenon. Change p1 in step `4` to another pod `p4`. p4 and p1 need the same resource `10Gi`, but p4's priority is the same as p2's, both are `medium-priority`. p4 also needs to wait 5 minutes to be scheduled to node0.

p4:
```
# p4.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: p4
spec:
  containers:
  - name: p4-container
    image: nginx
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: "10Gi"
  # Note that it is medium-priority like p2
  priorityClassName: medium-priority
```

I think pods of the same priority should not assume that resources are already occupied by the nominated node, because they are all of the same priority. This is unfair to the later pods of the same priority, and the resources required by the later pods may be sufficient, but they are assumed to be occupied by the previous pods.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c999f9d828009f0a535237aca74ce2e5f6a8088c/pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/framework.go#L1035-L1036

Hi @chengjoey, thanks for your help!
>  If I fix it according to 2, I think it will destroy some existing logic

You're right that if we clean all the nominated pods some logic will be broken.
So maybe we can consider:
1) The most direct way to fix the root cause (where the pod's `nominated_node_name` is not cleaned when itself can no longer be bound to the nominated node) is: When a later pod was bound to a node with nominated pods, check each nominated pod individually. If a pod cannot be bound on the node after the current pod is bound, its `nominated_node_name` should be cleaned.
2) Alternatively, we can register the relevent plugins to a new `UpdatePodNominatedNodeName` event. I noticed there are existing events like `UpdatePodLabel` and `UpdatePodScaleDown`, so adding a new event for this fine-grained update might be helpful. However, I'm doubting that `nominated_node_name` is a field managed by the scheduler, not the user, so maybe there're better solution to do this (trigger the pod is retried as soon some `nominated_node_name` is cleared).

> If I comment out `nodeInfoOut.AddPodInfo(pi)`, p1 can be scheduled to node0 immediately

That's true, but I think this should be kept because according to [the comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c999f9d828009f0a535237aca74ce2e5f6a8088c/pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/framework.go#L977C2-L977C82), the scheduler need two pass filter (one pass with nominated pods, one pass without) to make sure the decision is compatible with the nominated pods no matter they are scheduled to the nominated node or not. 

---

> I think pods of the same priority should not assume that resources are already occupied by the nominated node, because they are all of the same priority. 

In my opinion, this logic is sound. P1 not only arrives earlier but is also the one preempting other pods. Therefore, it seems reasonable to reserve some resources for it.

> This is unfair to the later pods of the same priority, and the resources required by the later pods may be sufficient, but they are assumed to be occupied by the previous pods.

I think this behavior is intentional (though I'm not sure), so removing it might disrupt existing logic. Maybe we should ask for member's idea on this.
Alternatively, this issue could be addressed by clearing the nominated_node_name of the previous pod, possibly via the fixes mentioned above.
@dom4ha @sanposhiho could this affect the discussions in #126858?

It's an interesting corner case.
So, the scheduler should regard the update event of Pods that clears the nominated node info as the Pod deletion event, but only effective for lower priority Pods. 

So, in this issue's example, when `p2`'s nominatedNodeName is cleared, we should regard the update event to `p2` as Pod/Delete, and move `p1` back to the activeQ. (The resource fit plugin, which should be registered as a unsched plugin of `p2` registers Pod/Delete event) 
And, let's say the scheduler also has `p4` that has the highest priority. `p4` shouldn't be requeued to activeQ. That's what I meant by "only effective for lower priority Pods".

> could this affect the discussions in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/126858?

My current take is that it's a requeueing (event handling) problem, not a preemption problem, and hence I'd say it's not much related to that enhancement, for now.
/cc @macsko
/assign @dom4ha

I think the issue deserves an update. I added triggering the update some time ago, but struggled to write tests that can simulate it.

The tests are there now, but I discovered that with QHints enabled, the the events are ignored, since they don't treat removal of nominated node name as a delete (or basically a change that can release resources). The fix in the fit plugin is obvious, but I need to go though other plugins and check whether and how they should be modified.

title: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Race condition setting pod resize status
body:
The kubelet updates the pod status by first generating the pod status based on its internal representation, and then [merging](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go#L1049) that with the latest status from the API, based on whether the Kubelet should be the source of truth for those fields.

Currently, the PodResizeStatus is not synced with the API server status, which means that whatever the Kubelet thinks the resize status should be will overwrite whatever PodResizeStatus is currently stored in the API server. This can lead to a race condition where the Kubelet has not yet seen a resize update, and clobbers the `Proposed` resize status.

I'm not sure exactly what the right behavior is here, but it probably needs to be an intelligent state transition, or may require comparing resource versions.

/sig node
/kind bug
/cc @vinaykul @thockin

title: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Pod Resize - resize stuck in "InProgress"
body:
### What happened?

I am trying the the feature gate "InPlacePodVerticalScaling". I tried on multiple environment/versions and the result is always the same. Resize is forever stuck in "InProgress". 

I followed the doc: https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/resize-container-resources/

### What did you expect to happen?

Resize field in pod status should go to `complete`

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Follow this doc: https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/resize-container-resources/

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

I tested with kubernetes version 1.27 and 1.29 with the same result.
containerd version being v1.6.28.

The 2 requirements being (from my understanding):
kubernetes >=v1.27
containerd >=v1.6.9


### Cloud provider

I tried on GKE and locally with Minikube


### OS version

mac sonoma 14.1.2 (m1)

nodes.body: /sig node
do you have any logs or detail info?

I don't have more info than this unfortunately. There are no logs, it is in `InProgress` state forever.

I tested it with minikube: `minikube start --kubernetes-version=v1.29.2 --feature-gates=InPlacePodVerticalScaling=true
`
when its in ``InProgress`` you can desc the pod I think, but that might lack of info as well..
Yes, i can `desc` the Pod. There are no related info on the resize unfortunately. Did you succeed to recreate the bug ?

Hi,

I think this is a feature request , not a bug. Perhaps what you are asking for is, to add value `complete` in resize field in the Pod's status to indicate completion of successful resize ? As it is today it is expected behaviour, `complete` is not a defined type  

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9043ce05c125091c0cb5519206fd90d311abd8c8/staging/src/k8s.io/api/core/v1/types.go#L3089-L3098

Related info on the resize can be observed through the allocatedResources values, those have been updated to reflect the new desired CPU requests. If allocatedResources.cpu is equal to resources.limits.cpu indicates that node was able to accommodate the increased CPU resource needs.

I hit a similar issue when I reproduced #124786. In this case, I set a too small value to the memory limit. Then, I hit the following error and the pod resize status got stuck in “InProgress”:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b5bc8025be6179ff49ea2edf654a6b855ae00119/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L743

I guess you also hit one of  failures in this [doPodResizeAction()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b5bc8025be6179ff49ea2edf654a6b855ae00119/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L664). In this case, you could see what happened only in the kubelet log.


In order to make the failures visible to users, more work seems necessary around `PodSyncResult` and `ReasonCache`:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b5bc8025be6179ff49ea2edf654a6b855ae00119/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L1977-L1978
Emitting events might be another option.


After hitting a failure here, the pod worker retries to resize the pod periodically at regular resyncing because no error is returned:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b5bc8025be6179ff49ea2edf654a6b855ae00119/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L1989
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b5bc8025be6179ff49ea2edf654a6b855ae00119/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L1493-L1494
So, the pod gets stuck in `InProgress`. I'm afraid I’m not sure whether this is an intended behavior or we should abort resizing because I haven't dug this feature yet.

/triage accepted
/assign @esotsal

~~The kubelet actually never touches the resize status field. The only reference is in PrepareForUpdate in the API server, which sets it to `InProgress`. It looks like this portion of the KEP was never really implemented.~~

PR #125654 will record an event when an error is raised from `doPodReiszeAction()`.

title: Reduce the daemonset controller Node event-handler code logic to avoid the callback function processing Node events too slowly.
body:
### What happened?

issue ref:https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/121474#issuecomment-1786835345

When the daemonset controller watches update Node events, due to the large number of Node events, the `NodeInformer` [pendingNotifications](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3e438c54a77ccf7b9e0aff924eb977031099cc2f/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/shared_informer.go#L876) ring buffer has more Node events to be processed, resulting in the Node EventHandler's Add/Update callback function being processed slowly.

### What did you expect to happen?

 We should rewrite the daemonset controller to the pattern where event-handler is as cheap as possible by simply putting stuff into queue. The queue then gives us deduplication for free and all the logic is then happening in the workers.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

When the cluster size is 5K, the daemonset pod cannot be quickly created on the node.

title: no defined semantics for EndpointSlices of type "FQDN"
body:
The API docs (and the end-user docs) state that "FQDN" is a valid value for EndpointSlice.AddressType, but nothing explains what the expected semantics of an FQDN slice are. And in fact, the expected semantics seem to be "[it gets ignored](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.26.0-rc.0/pkg/proxy/endpoints_test.go#L1590)".

We should document what FQDN slices are for, and if the answer is (and always will be) "nothing" then we should mark that value deprecated.

/assign @robscott 
/kind bug
/kind documentation
/sig network
/priority backlog

nodes.body:
> . And in fact, the expected semantics seem to be "[it gets ignored](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.26.0-rc.0/pkg/proxy/endpoints_test.go#L1590)".

that is kube-proxy but slices can be consumed by others.

However, I've tried to find the motivation or some use cases but I couldn't find them https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/84091

So this came out of an OpenShift bug, where a customer was expecting FQDN EndpointSlices to work basically like ExternalName services, except being able to specify multiple remote endpoints. But CoreDNS doesn't implement that, and I don't see any way that it _could_ implement that, because you can't have multiple CNAMEs attached to the same service DNS name. It seems like the only thing that would be able to handle FQDN slices in a useful way would be an L7 proxy?
xref https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/105172

> I don't see any way that it could implement that, because you can't have multiple CNAMEs attached to the same service DNS name. 

I think any implementation would have to involve "flattening" the endpoint FQDNS. e.g.

For a type A query of `example.default.svc.cluster.local.`

The following answer would be illegal in DNS, since there are two CNAMEs with the same name.
```
example.default.svc.cluster.local. CNAME fqdn1.example.com.
example.default.svc.cluster.local. CNAME fqdn2.example.com.
fqdn1.example.com. A  10.0.0.1
fqdn2.example.com. A 10.0.0.2
```
so instead the answer could be flattened to ...
```
example.default.svc.cluster.local. A  10.0.0.1
example.default.svc.cluster.local. A 10.0.0.2
```

This would be like treating the FQDN endpoints as ALIASes.  ALIAS afaik not being an official DNS spec concept, but implemented by various DNS servers more or less as an "invisible" CNAME.

> so instead the answer could be flattened to ...

Ah, true. You can't really resolve the FQDNs to IPs _ahead of time_ and have `example.default.svc.cluster.local` resolve to that list of IPs (this runs into all the same problems as attempting to do FQDN NetworkPolicies), but I suppose CoreDNS could implement it by looking up the FQDNs _at the point when someone tries to resolve `example.default.svc.cluster.local`_ and returning the aggregated list of results.
Could the cluster DNS service publish `SVCB` records rather than `CNAME`s?
ISTR we left this in as a nod towards being more general-purpose, but I can't honestlrecall why it was a good idea.

Agree with @thockin here. This came from the idea that EndpointSlices could be used by different applications for entirely independent purposes, published and consumed by custom implementations. In retrospect I don't think we had sufficiently clear use cases for this, and I don't know of any implementations that make use of this feature today.

What if two applications each decided to use `addressType: FQDN` but interpreted it in incompatible ways?

I don't think EndpointSlice is currently designed correctly to be extensible. (eg, `addressType` must be a registered type, so you're pretty limited in what sorts of "independent purposes" you could use EndpointSlices for)

> We should document what FQDN slices are for, and if the answer is (and always will be) "nothing" then we should mark that value deprecated.

We could also mark it as “reserved” (and even warn if it's used, until whatever release where we start using it in earnest).

Agree - we should mark it deprecated and return an API warning when it is used.  Seems like an easy one for a newish contrib to jump on!

/help-wanted
/triage accepted

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8c8a4cf3e4a18e97359ce750530a4fa27bbd3b88/pkg/registry/discovery/endpointslice/strategy.go#L91-L93

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8c8a4cf3e4a18e97359ce750530a4fa27bbd3b88/pkg/registry/discovery/endpointslice/strategy.go#L111-L114

I think we should rollback this deprecation - or maybe scope the use of FQDN type to only having a single entry.

Knative was planning on making use of the FQDN type to work around restrictions with Service type=ExternalName

The K8s CVE-2021-25740 mentions https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/103675

> A similar attack is possible using Ingress implementations that support forwarding to ExternalName Services. This can be used to forward to Services in other namespaces or, in some cases, sensitive endpoints within the Ingress implementation. If you are using the Ingress API, we recommend confirming that the implementation you’re using either does not support forwarding to ExternalName Services or supports disabling the functionality.

This was possible with Contour and hence they issued a CVE - https://github.com/projectcontour/contour/security/advisories/GHSA-5ph6-qq5x-7jwc restricting the feature.

With ingresses dropping support for ExternalName we were planning on [migrating](https://github.com/knative/serving/issues/11821) to using EndpointSlices with FQDN. The reasoning being is users don't interact with EndpointSlices and operators can use RBAC rules to limit their creation/modification - but allow the Knative control plane to do so.

Also an observation I noticed is that ingress implementations sorta ignored FQDN because when it became stable in K8s 1.21 it didn't actually work/did anything. It was only until CoreDNS 1.8.4 added support (which kubeadm used for K8s 1.22)  would FQDN act like a CNAME record.

I was also hoping ingress implementations (via the Gateway API) support these types of Services variants - by expanding their conformance tests - https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/issues/1718

> I was also hoping ingress implementations (via the Gateway API) support these types of Services variants - by expanding their conformance tests - [kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api#1718](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/issues/1718)

/cc @robscott

>With ingresses dropping support for ExternalName we were planning on https://github.com/knative/serving/issues/11821 to using EndpointSlices with FQDN. The reasoning being is users don't interact with EndpointSlices and operators can use RBAC rules to limit their creation/modification - but allow the Knative control plane to do so.

This does feel marginally safer, but I'm still not sure how safe it would be. Can you explain some of the specific use case(s) for FQDN addresses?

Knative creates K8s services of type external name which point to a cluster local proxy (typically the proxies service dns name - istio-ingressgateway.istio-system.svc.cluster.local). This allows us to perform L7 type routing within a cluster without a mesh.

> I think we should rollback this deprecation - or maybe scope the use of FQDN type to only having a single entry.

If there are use cases for new EndpointSlice AddressTypes, we could add them. (This would presumably require a KEP.) The problem is that there was no definition of what the existing FQDN type was supposed to mean.

But OTOH, do you actually need to be using `discoveryv1.EndpointSlice`? The slices you want aren't going to be automatically created by the EndpointSlice controller anyway... so why not just make a CRD type for the feature you want?

> If there are use cases for new EndpointSlice AddressTypes, we could add them. (This would presumably require a KEP.) The problem is that there was no definition of what the existing FQDN type was supposed to mean.

Why not backfill the use cases based on empirical usage - generally it seems like FQDN is being used to introduce CNAME records into Kubernetes's DNS services.

ie. using a kind cluster 1.22+
```yaml
apiVersion: discovery.k8s.io/v1
kind: EndpointSlice
metadata:
  name: helloworld
  labels:
    kubernetes.io/service-name: helloworld
addressType: FQDN
ports:
- name: http
  port: 80
  protocol: TCP
endpoints:
  - addresses:
      - "google.com"
    conditions:
      ready: true
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: helloworld
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  ports:
    - name: http
      protocol: TCP
      port: 80
```
```sh
$ kubectl run -ti --restart=Never --rm --image registry.k8s.io/e2e-test-images/jessie-dnsutils:1.3 dnsutils --  nslookup helloworld
Server:		10.96.0.10
Address:	10.96.0.10#53

helloworld.default.svc.cluster.local	canonical name = google.com.
Name:	google.com
Address: 142.251.33.174

pod "dnsutils" deleted
```

Here's an example of a downstream usage in practice - https://github.com/vmware-tanzu/cross-cluster-connectivity/issues/96

> But OTOH, do you actually need to be using discoveryv1.EndpointSlice? The slices you want aren't going to be automatically created by the EndpointSlice controller anyway... so why not just make a CRD type for the feature you want?

Unless I'm missing something - I don't see an alternative to EndpointSlices that let me provide DNS records to the cluster. I don't think creating a CRD is going to help here.

> generally it seems like FQDN is being used to introduce CNAME records into Kubernetes's DNS services.

see @chrisohaver comment in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/114210#issuecomment-1337646747

> The following answer would be illegal in DNS, since there are two CNAMEs with the same name.

However, it seems that it works in CoreDNS with one record, @chrisohaver any idea how this can work ? I can't see you process those types on CoreDNS
https://github.com/coredns/coredns/blob/915b74f2232573746bcc76e1e987775b076a9ef4/plugin/kubernetes/object/endpoint.go#L106
I'm wary of seeing CNAME as a big limitation, because we have records like SVCB likely to come available as standards. And we already have SRV.

So. This is a bit embarrassing. I’ve been following this and scratching my head because I don’t remember this being a feature of CoreDNS. I haven’t had time to confirm, but I think the CoreDNS behavior is  an unintentional result of how the endpointslice is passed to the “backend” to be rendered to a dns record. The backend renders any non-ip record value as a CNAME.

> generally it seems like FQDN is being used to introduce CNAME records into Kubernetes's DNS services

This seems more like a bug than an intentional feature.  We have a supported way of introducing a CNAME record - `Service.spec.type: ExternalName`.  We should not add another equivalent-but-different mechanism.

>> With ingresses dropping support for ExternalName we were planning on knative/serving#11821 to using EndpointSlices with FQDN. The reasoning being is users don't interact with EndpointSlices and operators can use RBAC rules to limit their creation/modification - but allow the Knative control plane to do so.
>
> This does feel marginally safer, but I'm still not sure how safe it would be. 

My thoughts exactly.  Epsilon safer than a literal CVE is not "safe".

> Knative creates K8s services of type external name which point to a cluster local proxy (typically the proxies service dns name - istio-ingressgateway.istio-system.svc.cluster.local). This allows us to perform L7 type routing within a cluster without a mesh.

And this works, right?  As long as you don't try to create an Ingress.

Let's recall what that CVE was about - it was about not letting user B expose user A's workloads to user C (canonical example of C being "the internet"). 

Thinking out loud: 

@robscott this kind of feels like a job for ReferenceGrant, doesn't it?

If one were to drop a refgrant into namespace `istio-system`, expressing "allow access to Service istio-ingressgateway from namespace *", it seems clearer that the controller should allow it.  But actually, wait.  That doesn't distinguish between internal and external use, and once you have access to the proxy, I guess it uses hostname routing?

So could I do this:

User A has a service X intended only for internal traffic, ExternalName = the cluster proxy.
User B creates a service Y, ExternalName = the cluster proxy
User B gives service Y an internet-facing Ingress, which gets IP 1.2.3.4
User C accesses 1.2.3.4 with the hostname header set to "x.a.svc.cluster.local" 

User B has done exactly what that CVE tried to prevent.

Changing ExternalName to FQDN EPSlice limits this only to users who can write EPSlices, which is a small consolation.  Fundamentally you have a shared proxy, whose routing instructions are in the attacker's hands (hostname).  That just can't work, unless the routing is taken out of the attacker's control (e.g. destination IP or port).

Please forgive me if I am making some incorrect leap in logic.

> This seems more like a bug than an intentional feature. 

Your bug is my feature ;)

> And this works, right? As long as you don't try to create an Ingress.

Yup it works but _now_ it depends on the ingress implementation and their posture towards Service type=ExternalName.

> My thoughts exactly. Epsilon safer than a literal CVE is not "safe". ... Changing ExternalName to FQDN EPSlice limits this only to users who can write EPSlices, which is a small consolation.

I think you're on point where users don't create Endpoint[Slice]s and operators can easily create RBAC rules to prevent them. Since the creation of EndpointSlice type=FQDN can be limited to control planes (ie. Knative) I hope ingress implementations feel confident routing to these types of Services by default.

> Please forgive me if I am making some incorrect leap in logic.

Your example doesn't really apply because Knative has a common use case where people create internal Knative Services and then expose a few them to the internet using a DomainMapping feature.  But we have complimentary resources for the operator to limit _who_ can create _what_ mappings.

For this to work we need affordances that Ingress implementations trust.

nodes.title: Try to clarify EndpointSlice semantics some more
nodes.body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
Jordan's review of #129837 pointed out some places where I was assuming the EndpointSlice semantics which are agreed upon by the EndpointSlice controller and kube-proxy, but which are not actually required by the API.

This is sort of a followup to #106267, trying to clarify the difference between "everything the EndpointSlice API lets you do" vs "how the EndpointSliceController and kube-proxy use the EndpointSlice API":

- EndpointSlices that correspond to Services must have a `"kubernetes.io/service-name"` label pointing back to their Service.
- An EndpointSlice can have `Ports: nil`, but the EndpointSlice controller only generates slices with at least one port, and kube-proxy only processes slices with at least one port.
- An EndpointPort can have `Port: nil`, but the EndpointSlice controller only generates slices with numeric ports, and kube-proxy only processes slices with numeric ports. I removed the claim that "If this is not specified, ports are not restricted" since nothing in k/k expects those semantics.
- An Endpoint can have multiple `Addresses`, but the EndpointSlice controller only generates slices with exactly 1 address, and kube-proxy only looks at the first address. I removed the claim that "These are all assumed to be fungible" since nothing in k/k expects those semantics.
- `AddressTypeFQDN` is deprecated and has no defined semantics (#114210).
- `Ready` is derived from `Serving`, not vice versa, as the docs implied for historical reasons.
- `Ready: nil` and `Serving: nil` mean "true". `Terminating: nil` means "false". There is no reason for making these "undefined". (Note that the docs previously claimed that "If [serving is] nil, consumers should defer to the ready condition" but this is not how kube-proxy interpreted it, so I changed it to match kube-proxy's interpretation.)

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
Fixes #114210 
and other stuff

```release-note
NONE
```

title: Pods not consistently being cleaned up
body:
### What happened?

We have a K8S 1.22.3 environment using containerd (no docker) where pods are not being consistently cleaned up. The basic idea is that we have a process that spawns several pods every couple of minutes, and those pods are subsequently deleted. They do not show up doing a 'kubectl get pods'. However, running 'crictl pods' shows that these pods sometimes stick around in a NotReady state. For example:

Feb 10 11:31:47 node1 kubelet[3123]: I0210 11:31:47.892981    3123 reconciler.go:224] "operationExecutor.VerifyControllerAttachedVolume started for volume \"tmp\" (UniqueName: \"kubernetes.io/empty-dir/8ce16f07-3fb3-42c5-ab0b-7b9c4b5c5672-tmp\") pod \"prepull-ds-nasjpdvl-lcbzp\" (UID: \"8ce16f07-3fb3-42c5-ab0b-7b9c4b5c5672\") "

In that case no NotReady pods stick around long term like we're seeing on 1.22.3. In case it's relevant, we also see a lot of the sandbox containers persisting:

```

title: CRI stats are overwritten by cAdvisor ones for Summary API
body:
### What happened?

I was going over the memory metrics being returned by Summary API based on the table that @haircommander built [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/2371-cri-pod-container-stats#current-fulfiller-of-metrics-endpoints--future-proposal). Notice that the provider for `container_memory_working_set_bytes` is listed as CRI. This appears to match what is being done in the code, as it's only `Memory.WorkingSetBytes` being picked up from the CRI stats for memory as seen here https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0153febd9f0098d4b8d0d484927710eaf899ef40/pkg/kubelet/stats/cri_stats_provider.go#L627-L635

So the outcome should be that `Memory.WorkingSetBytes` is provided by CRI and all the other memory metrics come from cAdvisor.

Let's take the case of a Kubernetes cluster running on containerd (e.g. like AKS does) and also assume that the `PodAndContainerStatsFromCRI` feature gate introduced in version 1.23 is not enabled. In turn the CRI provider will be created accordingly here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0153febd9f0098d4b8d0d484927710eaf899ef40/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L717-L727
Next let's consider the method here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0153febd9f0098d4b8d0d484927710eaf899ef40/pkg/kubelet/stats/cri_stats_provider.go#L270
Since we agreed that the `PodAndContainerStatsFromCRI` feature gate is not enabled, then the `if` block below doesn't run: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0153febd9f0098d4b8d0d484927710eaf899ef40/pkg/kubelet/stats/cri_stats_provider.go#L279-L305
We move forward and we retrieve the metrics from the containers via CRI here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0153febd9f0098d4b8d0d484927710eaf899ef40/pkg/kubelet/stats/cri_stats_provider.go#L307
Then we get the list of cAdvisor metrics a few lines further down: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0153febd9f0098d4b8d0d484927710eaf899ef40/pkg/kubelet/stats/cri_stats_provider.go#L312
Then we start iterating over the metrics returned by the CRI, and we first process the CRI metrics. Next pod stats are updated via this method: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0153febd9f0098d4b8d0d484927710eaf899ef40/pkg/kubelet/stats/cri_stats_provider.go#L528
Now this is where it gets interesting: since cAdvisor most likely will return data for every single container - the following line runs: 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0153febd9f0098d4b8d0d484927710eaf899ef40/pkg/kubelet/stats/cri_stats_provider.go#L349
Inside `addCadvisorContainerCPUAndMemoryStats` the container data that was previously returned from CRI (`cs.Memory`) appears to be wiped out by the cAdvisor data here https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0153febd9f0098d4b8d0d484927710eaf899ef40/pkg/kubelet/stats/cri_stats_provider.go#L894-L909

But since going through the code is error-prone, I followed the advice from @dashpole and used a unit test. Running the `TestCRIListPodCPUAndMemoryStats` in [cri_stats_provider_test.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/38ec822b46853acfb3c3dc7e386a8d4636c67e03/pkg/kubelet/stats/cri_stats_provider_test.go#L435) gives the following outcome for one of the containers:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/31319583/147010219-814f6298-db77-4e47-a81d-9e5511b91ffe.png)

`containerStats0` contains the initial CRI mock memory metric data, `infos` is the map the contains the initial cAdvisor mock data, while c0 is one of the results of running the `ListPodCPUAndMemoryStats` method. Notice that the initial value for `WorkingSetBytes` is no longer present in the output.

### What did you expect to happen?

The `WorkingSetBytes` should have been picked up based on the CRI stats, not cAdvisor ones.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run the unit test indicated in the original description.

### Anything else we need to know?

Building and testing were done on a Windows 10 box (21H1) running JetBrains GoLand 2021.2.4 configured to use an Ubuntu 20.04 instance running under WSL2 as its compile and test target.

### Kubernetes version

I've tested on the current `master` branch, but the same outcome is seen with tag `v1.21.1`.

### Cloud provider

Not relevant

### OS version

_No response_

### Install tools

_No response_

### Container runtime (CRI) and and version (if applicable)

_No response_

### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

_No response_

I reproduced this issue in unit tests where the value of the `Memory.WorkingSetBytes` field was indeed overridden by the value of Cadvisor.

Recently I was looking at this part of the Summary API  logic and I wanted to try to fix it.
/assign

/cc @haircommander @bobbypage

It should be this place that calls `p.addCadvisorContainerCPUAndMemoryStats(cs, &caStats)` to overwrite the statistics obtained from CRI:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c75d254beb662ea73736d2f123d0382b7f91dfbd/pkg/kubelet/stats/cri_stats_provider.go#L343-L350
/sig node

/assign @haircommander

@haircommander can you please triage?

/triage accepted
/priority important-longterm

I have checked with a fresh perspective from break, and I do think this is a bug, especially because it affects older versions that don't have the PodAndContainerStatsFromCRI option.

There does exist the argument that it has been the intention of CRI stats for a while to be supplemented by cAdvisor with fields that the CRI didn't define, but WorkingSetBytes is overridden here https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0153febd9f0098d4b8d0d484927710eaf899ef40/pkg/kubelet/stats/helper.go#L62 so there is virtually no point to calling for the CRI stats.

I would either expect the cAdvisor stats to be applied before the CRI, so CRI wins, or the CRI fields to not be specified by the function translating from cAdvisor stats. I expect the former to be simpler. Did you want to take this on @mengjiao-liu  ?

> I would either expect the cAdvisor stats to be applied before the CRI, so CRI wins, or the CRI fields to not be specified by the function translating from cAdvisor stats. I expect the former to be simpler. 

I agree with you, the first way is simpler.

And I want take this to better understand the logic of the summary API. I estimate that I will work on this one this week or next.
/assign @mengjiao-liu

Thanks for catching this @luckerby. A couple questions:

1. Is cAdvisor stats overriding CRI stats consistent with previous behavior? Or is this is a behavior change / regression in 1.23?
2. Are there other fields which have the same behavior, e.g. CPU where stats are obtained by both CRI and cAdvisor and cAdvisor stats override the CRI stats?

@bobbypage For (1) I didn't quite remember, but just saw that in my original post I did mention seeing similar outcomes with  `v1.21.1` when running the same unit test.
For (2) I only focused on memory, but by the looks of the code and the fact that memory and CPU stats are treated rather similarly, I would expect at least CPU stats to have the same problem. Not sure about other stats, and I'd have to defer to those more experienced with the code.
Got it, thanks for the info. We should check (1) so we can understand if this a regression or if this has been the behavior all along.

> Is cAdvisor stats overriding CRI stats consistent with previous behavior? Or is this is a behavior change / regression in 1.23?

I checked the git history and added the following code is in kubernetes 1.13 version.
This part of the logic should not have changed, so the  CRI stats data may not have been correctly obtained from the CRI from the beginning.

PR: #68841
commit: 3b21995c951f551d3c16fa4e38cbb21836e242c7
Due to vacation, the time to fix this issue has been extended, if others are interested, you can fix it first.
The vacation is over, I will continue to work on this issue.

> Thanks for catching this @luckerby. A couple questions:
> 
> 2. Are there other fields which have the same behavior, e.g. CPU where stats are obtained by both CRI and cAdvisor and cAdvisor stats override the CRI stats?

I found an issue related with this. Because some fields(RSSBytes/ UsageCoreNanoSeconds) are missing in stats got from cAdvisor, so after overwrite, these fields are missing when exposed by summary API. 

Could I only trust the stats from cri and skip the step to get stats from cadvisor?

title: kubectl get pods command shows status AppArmor for pod on k8s v1.22
body:
#### What happened:
I recently upgraded to k8s version 1.22 and made the following observations. I deployed hello-apparmor.yaml example from the kubernetes tutorial on [securing pods with AppArmor](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tutorials/clusters/apparmor/).
hello-apparmor.yaml
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: hello-apparmor
  annotations:
    container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/hello: localhost/k8s-apparmor-example-deny-write
spec:
  containers:
  - name: hello
    image: busybox
    command: [ "sh", "-c", "echo 'Hello AppArmor!' && sleep 1h" ]
```
Since I had not loaded corresponding apparmor profile yet I got this output using `kubectl describe pods`:
```
Annotations:  container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/hello: localhost/k8s-apparmor-example-deny-write
Status:       Pending
Reason:       AppArmor
Message:      Cannot enforce AppArmor: profile "k8s-apparmor-example-deny-write" is not loaded
```
And `kubectl get pods -A` output:
```
vagrant@ubuntu-focal:~$ kubectl get po -A
NAMESPACE     NAME                                   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS      AGE
default       hello-apparmor                         0/1     Blocked   0             4s
kube-system   cilium-9x8xr                           1/1     Running   1 (19h ago)   20h
kube-system   cilium-operator-58874d67c7-lxwmq       1/1     Running   1 (10m ago)   20h
kube-system   coredns-78fcd69978-msf42               1/1     Running   1 (10m ago)   20h
kube-system   coredns-78fcd69978-tjvgd               1/1     Running   1 (19h ago)   20h
kube-system   etcd-ubuntu-focal                      1/1     Running   2 (10m ago)   20h
kube-system   kube-apiserver-ubuntu-focal            1/1     Running   2 (10m ago)   20h
kube-system   kube-controller-manager-ubuntu-focal   1/1     Running   2 (10m ago)   20h
kube-system   kube-proxy-894v8                       1/1     Running   1 (10m ago)   20h
kube-system   kube-scheduler-ubuntu-focal            1/1     Running   2 (19h ago)   20h
```
So to correct that I applied the desired apparmor profile(k8s-apparmor-example-deny-write). After doing so I get the following outputs:
`sudo aa-status`
```
30 profiles are in enforce mode.
   /snap/snapd/12883/usr/lib/snapd/snap-confine
   /snap/snapd/12883/usr/lib/snapd/snap-confine//mount-namespace-capture-helper
   /usr/bin/man
   /usr/lib/NetworkManager/nm-dhcp-client.action
   /usr/lib/NetworkManager/nm-dhcp-helper
   /usr/lib/connman/scripts/dhclient-script
   /usr/lib/snapd/snap-confine
   /usr/lib/snapd/snap-confine//mount-namespace-capture-helper
   /usr/sbin/tcpdump
   /{,usr/}sbin/dhclient
   docker-default
   k8s-apparmor-example-deny-write
```
`kubectl describe pods`
```
vagrant@ubuntu-focal:~$ kubectl get po -A
NAMESPACE     NAME                                   READY   STATUS     RESTARTS      AGE
default       hello-apparmor                         1/1     AppArmor   0             6m28s
kube-system   cilium-9x8xr                           1/1     Running    1 (19h ago)   20h
kube-system   cilium-operator-58874d67c7-lxwmq       1/1     Running    1 (16m ago)   20h
kube-system   coredns-78fcd69978-msf42               1/1     Running    1 (16m ago)   20h
kube-system   coredns-78fcd69978-tjvgd               1/1     Running    1 (19h ago)   20h
kube-system   etcd-ubuntu-focal                      1/1     Running    2 (16m ago)   20h
kube-system   kube-apiserver-ubuntu-focal            1/1     Running    2 (16m ago)   20h
kube-system   kube-controller-manager-ubuntu-focal   1/1     Running    2 (16m ago)   20h
kube-system   kube-proxy-894v8                       1/1     Running    1 (16m ago)   20h
kube-system   kube-scheduler-ubuntu-focal            1/1     Running    2 (19h ago)   20h
```
`kubectl describe pods`
```
Annotations:  container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/hello: localhost/k8s-apparmor-example-deny-write
Status:       Running
Reason:       AppArmor
Message:      Cannot enforce AppArmor: profile "k8s-apparmor-example-deny-write" is not loaded
```
#### What you expected to happen:
I followed the same steps on k8s version 1.21 and couldn't produce the issue. I think we should get `Running` instead of `AppArmor` and the message shouldn't be displayed since the profile is already applied.
#### How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):
Steps to reproduce:
1. Deploy a pod with apparmor annotations.
2. Enforce the associated apparmor profile.
#### Anything else we need to know?:
1. I checked whether profile is actually being enforced using `kubectl exec -ti hello-apparmor -- /bin/sh` and found that the profile is indeed enforced on the pod containers.
```
/ # touch newfile
touch: newfile: Permission denied
```
Here I tried creating newfile and apparmor blocks it since the profile denies write.
2. This doesn't go away even after waiting for several hours.
#### Environment:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`):
```
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"22", GitVersion:"v1.22.0", GitCommit:"c2b5237ccd9c0f1d600d3072634ca66cefdf272f", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2021-08-04T18:03:20Z", GoVersion:"go1.16.6", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}

```

title: List watch request for Events with stale resourceVersion responds immediately without error
body:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!

If the matter is security related, please disclose it privately via https://kubernetes.io/security/
-->


#### What happened:
Per the [documentation on using watches](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/#efficient-detection-of-changes) I attempted to resume a timed out watch for `events.k8s.io/v1` `Event` objects by issuing a new List request with the `watch` parameter set and the `resourceVersion` set to the last `Event` object I'd received on the watch.

However, by the time I issued the new request that `resourceVersion` was stale.  The response I received from the K8S API was an immediate HTTP 200 with an empty request body.  (This confused the K8S library I was using which was expecting a 410 Gone error in that case, and resulted in a busy-loop of retrying over and over which put strain on the K8S API server.)

#### What you expected to happen:
I expected the watch request to receive a response with some form of `410 Gone` error (either in the HTTP status code or as some form of JSON error object in the response body).  This is the documented behavior, and I was able to verify that this is what happens for other resource types like Secrets.

#### How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):

##### How to reproduce the failure for Events
Ensure there are recorded events in the Kubernetes cluster, e.g., `kubectl -n YOUR-NS-HERE get events.events.k8s.io` yields a non-empty output.

Then request a watch for events with a known stale `resourceVersion`.
```
$ curl -i -kE k3s.client.pem 'https://localhost:6443/apis/events.k8s.io/v1/namespaces/YOUR-NS-HERE/events?&watch=1&resourceVersion=1'      
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Cache-Control: no-cache, private
Content-Type: application/json
Date: Thu, 05 Aug 2021 15:58:57 GMT
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

```

Note that even though the `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` header is given, the K8S API server closes the connection immediately after serving an empty response.

##### How to reproduce correct behavior for an alternate Resource type (e.g., a Secret)
```
$ curl -i -kE k3s.client.pem 'https://localhost:6443/api/v1/namespaces/YOUR-NS-HERE/secrets?&watch=true&resourceVersion=1'                                                                                                          HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Cache-Control: no-cache, private
Content-Type: application/json
Date: Thu, 05 Aug 2021 15:58:40 GMT
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

{"type":"ERROR","object":{"kind":"Status","apiVersion":"v1","metadata":{},"status":"Failure","message":"too old resource version: 1 (1126176)","reason":"Expired","code":410}}
```

#### Anything else we need to know?:

#### Environment:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`):
```
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"21", GitVersion:"v1.21.3", GitCommit:"ca643a4d1f7bfe34773c74f79527be4afd95bf39", GitTreeState:"archive", BuildDate:"2021-07-16T17:16:46Z", GoVersion:"go1.16.5", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"21", GitVersion:"v1.21.2+k3s1", GitCommit:"5a67e8dc473f8945e8e181f6f0b0dbbc387f6fca", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2021-06-21T20:52:44Z", GoVersion:"go1.16.4", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
```
I have also tested and verified this bug exists in Kubernetes 1.19.12.
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration: MacBook Pro running Kubernetes locally on Linux
- OS (e.g: `cat /etc/os-release`):
```
NAME="Arch Linux"
PRETTY_NAME="Arch Linux"
ID=arch
BUILD_ID=rolling
ANSI_COLOR="38;2;23;147;209"
HOME_URL="https://archlinux.org/"
DOCUMENTATION_URL="https://wiki.archlinux.org/"
SUPPORT_URL="https://bbs.archlinux.org/"
BUG_REPORT_URL="https://bugs.archlinux.org/"
LOGO=archlinux
```
- Kernel (e.g. `uname -a`): `Linux redacted 5.10.55-1-lts #1 SMP Sat, 31 Jul 2021 08:12:13 +0000 x86_64 GNU/Linux`
- Install tools: [Arch Linux AUR package for K3S 1.21](https://aur.archlinux.org/packages/k3s-1.21-bin/)
- Network plugin and version (if this is a network-related bug):
- Others:

(Please forgive me if that's not the right SIG, but it looked like the closest match from the SIG list to me.)

Copy from the doc: https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/#watch-bookmarks
```
When the requested watch operations fail because `the historical version of that resource is not available`, clients must handle the case by recognizing the status code 410 Gone, clearing their local cache, performing a list operation, and starting the watch from the resourceVersion returned by that new list operation. 
```
To my understanding, `410 Gone` only means that the client requests a resourceVersion older than the server has retained rather than the resourceVersion is stale.

@YouHang: My choice of words could have been better.  When I wrote that a `resourceVersion` was "stale" what I meant was that the `resourceVersion` was expired and no longer retained by the API Server.  Hopefully this is made more clear if you closely examine the reproduction example I gave which uses a parameter `resourceVersion=1`, a choice explicitly intended to never be recognized as recent by a K8S server.

So in the case I am describing, `410 Gone` very much is the response that should be generated according to the documentation and as illustrated by other resources like `Secret` exhibiting that behavior.  But for `Event` resources this is not happening.

/assign @jpbetz 
/triage accepted

I noticed that the failing watch request had "watch=1". I'm not familiar using 1 as the value of that parameter (vs. the more common "watch=true" is usages I've seen). Have you attempted this with `watch=true`?
@jpbetz: Yes, `watch=1` and `watch=true` yield the same behavior.  The Event listing response stream still closes immediately instead of staying open for the server-defined timeout period.

title: Re-entrant apiserver calls are not part of the same trace
body:
Part of enhancement: kubernetes/enhancements#647

This is a continuation of the discussion in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/94942#discussion_r657114027, which was a discussion of the risks of abuse that might be possible   To summarize, the [`otelhttp.WithPublicEndpoint()`](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go-contrib/blob/6d226aff737e650125fd98e18ccba66428f328f7/instrumentation/net/http/otelhttp/config.go#L103) option causes spans generated by the API Server handler to be the start of a new trace (with a link to the incoming trace), rather than be children of the incoming request.

Note: I think there is a bug in OpenTelemetry in which parent contexts are still used for sampling decisions: https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go/issues/2031.  I'll make sure that is fixed separately.

However, one of the use-cases outlined in the [KEP](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-instrumentation/647-apiserver-tracing#tracing-api-requests) is tracing reentrant API calls.  Using WithPublicEndpoint make reentrant calls difficult to visualize, because they are each their own trace now.  We should probably keep the default behavior as using WithPublicEndpoint, but expose an option to make it non-public.  But first, we should discuss and document what the abuse implications are for an actor with the ability to send requests to the kubernetes API with a span context.  The implications discussed thus far are:

* If the actor has access to the Trace ID from another trace, they can append spans to it.  This wouldn't impact any other spans in the trace, but would append the span to the trace.
* The actor can set sampled=true in their request to cause the apiserver to record spans for all of their requests.  They could potentially overwhelm a tracing backend, or cause other spans to be dropped.

One unanswered question from the thread from @liggitt:
> @lavalamp, you've thought about the abuse vectors more w.r.t. priority and fairness... do you have thoughts on this?

We should never be adding to user-controlled traces, IMO.

apiserver should add baggage to its trace headers. Rentrant calls should repeat the baggage. Then the 2nd apiserver can use this to verify that the trace was originated by some apiserver in the cluster. In that case, it should append to a trace. Otherwise, it should start a new one. This should not be an option for the user. There are multiple ways of constructing such a baggage value.

If you have a strong use case for a user starting a trace, let me know, but I don't think it's going to outweigh the anti-abuse perspective.

> If you have a strong use case for a user starting a trace, let me know, but I don't think it's going to outweigh the anti-abuse perspective.

I'd like to be able to run `kubectl apply -f blah.yaml --trace` but I am indifferent as to whether that actually attaches a trace directly or runs through some webhook which validates who i am and then attaches a trace to the request.

I don't see how webhooks could attach a trace.

Letting users request apiserver initiate a trace is different than attaching a request to an already created trace, no?

If we let users request extra resource usage (trace allocation), then IMO we have to authz that somehow.

Maybe I'm phrasing this incorrectly. We can have some mechanism by which either kubectl attaches a trace header directly, or attaches some sort of proxy pseudo trace header which the apiserver can then, after authz-ing (via a webhook or whatever), decide to actually attach a trace to the request.

Maybe a preexisting trace makes sense if folks are using api calls.

I guess my concern is just bounding the resource usage. A non-authz
solution might look like a cap on the %age of requests that get traced, and
user-requested traces count against that cap (and are ignored if it would
put it over the cap).

I don't think it works this way, but I definitely don't want apiserver
dialing out to some user-controlled address to report on a trace.

> Maybe I'm phrasing this incorrectly. We can have some mechanism by which
> either kubectl attaches a trace header directly, or attaches some sort of

>

> I don't think it works this way, but I definitely don't want apiserver

Yeah that's not really what I was saying.

> I guess my concern is just bounding the resource usage. A non-authz

cc @Richabanker

Would an acceptable solution be to have an option for internal-api-endpoints? If I have network-boundary around my apiserver, then I trust incoming traceparent headers and would propagate the headers? 

Including that as a command argument or part of the tracingconfiguration seem reasonable. If someone suggests a path that would be accepted, I'll happily take on implementing it.

That is a reasonable approach.  We need to think about:

* Should this only exist in the apiserver config?  Or is it applicable to all kubernetes components, and belong in component-base?
* Do we need per-http-server configuration, or is a single option enough? IIRC, there was more than one http server instrumented for apiserver tracing.

A related use case I have is I want to debug [some issues that appear in tests](https://github.com/knative/pkg/issues/1509) when my webhooks are invoked - they return a 200 response but the API server is failing and returning an EOF context timeout.

To debug this I would like the trace to start when the test makes the call to the API server. For this to be useful I would expect the API server to attach the trace context to outgoing requests.

If I could enable this cluster wide for testing/debugging purposes that would be great.

nodes.title: APIServerTracing: Respect trace context only for privileged users
nodes.body:
Second attempt at https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/123807, but including system:monitoring

### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Move the tracing filter to after the authorization filter, and only respect the incoming context for requests from the privileged `system:master` and `system:monitoring` groups.

This has some downsides:

* Tracing from authorization isn't part of the APIServer trace

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
Fixes https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/103186

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

See discussions in:
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/94942#discussion_r657114027
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/103186#issuecomment-1970288470

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
Respect the incoming trace context for authenticated requests to the kube-apiserver for APIServer tracing.
```

#### Additional documentation e.g., KEPs (Kubernetes Enhancement Proposals), usage docs, etc.:

```docs
- [KEP]: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-instrumentation/0034-distributed-tracing-kep.md
```

title: yaml may fail to parse spuriously
body:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!

If the matter is security related, please disclose it privately via https://kubernetes.io/security/
-->


**What happened**: JSON with comments in it (IE Yaml) will be "detected" as JSON because it matches `^\s+{.*` in the first 100 bytes and be parsed as JSON even though it is valid YAML instead.

**What you expected to happen**: We should parse valid YAML as YAML. We should probably parse everything as YAML since it is a superset of JSON.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

**Anything else we need to know?**:

The code is here:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/14e322cc827ca546eb80b721a825a43311a99437/pkg/util/yaml/decoder.go#L202

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/14e322cc827ca546eb80b721a825a43311a99437/pkg/util/yaml/decoder.go#L305-L327

Thread in slack: https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C13J86Z63/p1560351860082800

**Environment**: n/a

cc @smarterclayton @dims @liggitt @Katharine @chuckha 
/sig apimachinery

nodes.body: /sig api-machinery

Are there any downsides to tidying this up to all be parsed as YAML, or do we need to go in and make the GuessJSONStream a bit better at differentiating between the two? Either way I'd be willing to take a crack at this as my first issue, with a little direction, if it's still free for the taking.

This is what @smarterclayton had to say in the slack thread linked above.

...

claytonc  [1 hour ago]
they were in streaming contexts

claytonc  [1 hour ago]
did we have a streaming yaml parser?  i think there was a reason we couldn’t use it at the time

claytonc  [1 hour ago]
we need the raw yaml to pass to the deserializer for sure

claytonc  [1 hour ago]
this predates the streaming deserializers which probably would support this correctly now

claytonc  [1 hour ago]
we would need a yaml framer and i don’t see one in the codebase

claytonc  [1 hour ago]
if yaml has a RawExtension equivalent that would work

...

claytonc  [26 minutes ago]
it’s definitely a bug, it’s probably not an easy fix (well, the correct fix is not easy)

...

> We should probably parse everything as YAML since it is a superset of JSON.

we need to be *super* sure that doesn't regress performance or correctness (some yaml-related normalization issues at https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/73655 and https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/yaml/pull/14)

> we need to be super sure that doesn't regress performance or correctness (some yaml-related normalization issues at #73655 and kubernetes-sigs/yaml#14)

performance I can see, but _we don't have correctness_ currently?

> but we don't have correctness currently?

There are several yaml->json helper methods, and I don't know the state of all of them w.r.t. numeric parsing (parse to float64? uint64? int?) and handling of edge cases (xref https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/yaml/pull/14#discussion_r271939039). We just need to be sure we're not switching to something that accepts data it shouldn't or loses round-trip information.

> We should probably parse everything as YAML since it is a superset of JSON.

When accepting an API request that claims to contain json, we should not parse it as yaml

> There are several yaml->json helper methods, and I don't know the state of all of them w.r.t. numeric parsing (parse to float64? uint64? int?) and handling of edge cases (xref kubernetes-sigs/yaml#14 (comment)). We just need to be sure we're not switching to something that accepts data it shouldn't or loses round-trip information.

:+1: 

> > We should probably parse everything as YAML since it is a superset of JSON.
>
> When accepting an API request that claims to contain json, we should not parse it as yaml

To be fair, that's not happening at this layer, this layer _only_ looks at the content bytes and decides to parse based on that. If we are explicitly told it's JSON at some higher layer hopefully we aren't using this code at all.
/cc @apelisse @jennybuckley

Do we know exactly where the data is coming from when we're trying to guess the format? My understanding is that this should not happen when reading from http request since I would expect the content-type to be set (or defaulted to a value, rather than guessed ... maybe that's the problem).

Recognizers should only be applied when it is impossible to know the content type (storage, random files on disk and user is a jerk).  We'd need to assuage jordan's concerns about correctness (mine too) before we switch to be all YAML.  YAML has more unbounded processing bugs too which means there may be states in storage that are not great.

Switching decoder of CRD to allowing YAML is not something I'd want, so we'd have to verify the deserializers in storage only allow proto or JSON.
Trying to think if there is any way flipping this for disk reads of files would break someone's automation.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130199 should solve this

> https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130199 should solve this

It does for https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/78946#issuecomment-501439019, though I suspect we should break out that fix and merge it while we drive agreement on the other part https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130199#issuecomment-2707986663

This should be finally fixed by https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130666, which will ship in 1.33 🎉 
/assign @thockin 

Unclear if we should cherry-pick this, I kinda lean towards yes, on the other hand this is a very old bug and we'll probably have to assume clusters out there have it for the immediate future regardless. It might shorten that window a bit.
I don't think this qualifies for a backport.  Not that I am not confident in it, but the risk is >> reward.
